93: // DeferredBatchOp represents a batch operation (eg. set, merge, delete) that is
94: // being inserted into the batch. Indexing is not performed on the specified key
95: // until Finish is called, hence the name deferred. This struct lets the caller
96: // copy or encode keys/values directly into the batch representation instead of
97: // copying into an intermediary buffer then having pebble.Batch copy off of it.
98: type DeferredBatchOp struct {
99: 	index *batchskl.Skiplist
100: 
101: 	// Key and Value point to parts of the binary batch representation where
102: 	// keys and values should be encoded/copied into. len(Key) and len(Value)
103: 	// bytes must be copied into these slices respectively before calling
104: 	// Finish(). Changing where these slices point to is not allowed.
105: 	Key, Value []byte
106: 	offset     uint32
107: }
108: 
109: // Finish completes the addition of this batch operation, and adds it to the
110: // index if necessary. Must be called once (and exactly once) keys/values
111: // have been filled into Key and Value. Not calling Finish or not
112: // copying/encoding keys will result in an incomplete index, and calling Finish
113: // twice may result in a panic.
114: func (d DeferredBatchOp) Finish() error {
115: 	if d.index != nil {
116: 		if err := d.index.Add(d.offset); err != nil {
117: 			return err
118: 		}
119: 	}
120: 	return nil
121: }

123: // A Batch is a sequence of Sets, Merges, Deletes, DeleteRanges, RangeKeySets,
124: // RangeKeyUnsets, and/or RangeKeyDeletes that are applied atomically. Batch
125: // implements the Reader interface, but only an indexed batch supports reading
126: // (without error) via Get or NewIter. A non-indexed batch will return
127: // ErrNotIndexed when read from. A batch is not safe for concurrent use, and
128: // consumers should use a batch per goroutine or provide their own
129: // synchronization.
130: //
131: // # Indexing
132: //
133: // Batches can be optionally indexed (see DB.NewIndexedBatch). An indexed batch
134: // allows iteration via an Iterator (see Batch.NewIter). The iterator provides
135: // a merged view of the operations in the batch and the underlying
136: // database. This is implemented by treating the batch as an additional layer
137: // in the LSM where every entry in the batch is considered newer than any entry
138: // in the underlying database (batch entries have the InternalKeySeqNumBatch
139: // bit set). By treating the batch as an additional layer in the LSM, iteration
140: // supports all batch operations (i.e. Set, Merge, Delete, DeleteRange,
141: // RangeKeySet, RangeKeyUnset, RangeKeyDelete) with minimal effort.
142: //
143: // The same key can be operated on multiple times in a batch, though only the
144: // latest operation will be visible. For example, Put("a", "b"), Delete("a")
145: // will cause the key "a" to not be visible in the batch. Put("a", "b"),
146: // Put("a", "c") will cause a read of "a" to return the value "c".
147: //
148: // The batch index is implemented via an skiplist (internal/batchskl). While
149: // the skiplist implementation is very fast, inserting into an indexed batch is
150: // significantly slower than inserting into a non-indexed batch. Only use an
151: // indexed batch if you require reading from it.
152: //
153: // # Atomic commit
154: //
155: // The operations in a batch are persisted by calling Batch.Commit which is
156: // equivalent to calling DB.Apply(batch). A batch is committed atomically by
157: // writing the internal batch representation to the WAL, adding all of the
158: // batch operations to the memtable associated with the WAL, and then
159: // incrementing the visible sequence number so that subsequent reads can see
160: // the effects of the batch operations. If WriteOptions.Sync is true, a call to
161: // Batch.Commit will guarantee that the batch is persisted to disk before
162: // returning. See commitPipeline for more on the implementation details.
163: //
164: // # Large batches
165: //
166: // The size of a batch is limited to 4GB, the max that can be represented by
167: // a uint32 type. Be aware that indexed batches require considerably more
168: // memory for the skiplist structure (this skiplist is separate from the 4GB
169: // batch limit). For users that require atomic writes of data that's greater
170: // than 4GB, DB.Ingest() is able to atomically ingest pre-computed sstables.
171: // A given WAL file has a single memtable associated with it (this restriction
172: // could be removed, but doing so is onerous and complex). And a memtable has
173: // a fixed size due to the underlying fixed size arena. Note that this differs
174: // from RocksDB where a memtable can grow arbitrarily large using a list of
175: // arena chunks. In RocksDB this is accomplished by storing pointers in the
176: // arena memory, but that isn't possible in Go.
177: //
178: // During Batch.Commit, a batch which is larger than a threshold (>
179: // MemTableSize/2) is wrapped in a flushableBatch and inserted into the queue
180: // of memtables. A flushableBatch forces WAL to be rotated, but that happens
181: // anyways when the memtable becomes full so this does not cause significant
182: // WAL churn. Because the flushableBatch is readable as another layer in the
183: // LSM, Batch.Commit returns as soon as the flushableBatch has been added to
184: // the queue of memtables.
185: //
186: // Internally, a flushableBatch provides Iterator support by sorting the batch
187: // contents (the batch is sorted once, when it is added to the memtable
188: // queue). Sorting the batch contents and insertion of the contents into a
189: // memtable have the same big-O time, but the constant factor dominates
190: // here. Sorting is significantly faster and uses significantly less memory.
191: //
192: // # Internal representation
193: //
194: // WARNING: Do not remove the ability to handle older internal
195: // representations, without thinking through the consequences in CockroachDB.
196: // Specifically, CockroachDB can have unapplied raft log entries that contain
197: // encoded Pebble batches, and without a CockroachDB-level below-Raft
198: // migration they can correspond to arbitrarily old binary versions. Pebble
199: // needs to be able to successfully apply such batches.
200: //
201: // The internal batch representation is a contiguous byte buffer with a fixed
202: // 12-byte header, followed by a series of records.
203: //
204: //	+-------------+------------+--- ... ---+
205: //	| SeqNum (8B) | Count (4B) |  Entries  |
206: //	+-------------+------------+--- ... ---+
207: //
208: // Each record has a 1-byte kind tag prefix, followed by 1 or 2 length prefixed
209: // strings (varstring):
210: //
211: //	+-----------+-----------------+-------------------+
212: //	| Kind (1B) | Key (varstring) | Value (varstring) |
213: //	+-----------+-----------------+-------------------+
214: //
215: // A varstring is a varint32 followed by N bytes of data. The Kind tags are
216: // exactly those specified by InternalKeyKind. The following table shows the
217: // format for records of each kind:
218: //
219: //	InternalKeyKindDelete             varstring
220: //	InternalKeyKindLogData        	  varstring
221: //	InternalKeyKindIngestSST          varstring
222: //	InternalKeyKindIngestSSTWithBlobs varstring varstring (value contains blob file IDs)
223: //	InternalKeyKindSet                varstring varstring
224: //	InternalKeyKindMerge              varstring varstring
225: //	InternalKeyKindRangeDelete        varstring varstring
226: //	InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet        varstring varstring
227: //	InternalKeyKindRangeKeyUnset      varstring varstring
228: //	InternalKeyKindRangeKeyDelete     varstring varstring
229: //
230: // The intuitive understanding here are that the arguments to Delete, Set,
231: // Merge, DeleteRange and RangeKeyDelete are encoded into the batch. The
232: // RangeKeySet and RangeKeyUnset operations are slightly more complicated,
233: // encoding their end key, suffix and value [in the case of RangeKeySet] within
234: // the Value varstring. For more information on the value encoding for
235: // RangeKeySet and RangeKeyUnset, see the internal/rangekey package.
236: //
237: // The internal batch representation is the on disk format for a batch in the
238: // WAL, and thus stable. New record kinds may be added, but the existing ones
239: // will not be modified.
240: type Batch struct {
241: 	batchInternal
242: 	applied atomic.Bool
243: 	// lifecycle is used to negotiate the lifecycle of a Batch. A Batch and its
244: 	// underlying batchInternal.data byte slice may be reused. There are two
245: 	// mechanisms for reuse:
246: 	//
247: 	// 1. The caller may explicitly call [Batch.Reset] to reset the batch to be
248: 	//    empty (while retaining the underlying repr's buffer).
249: 	// 2. The caller may call [Batch.Close], passing ownership off to Pebble,
250: 	//    which may reuse the batch's memory to service new callers to
251: 	//    [DB.NewBatch].
252: 	//
253: 	// There's a complication to reuse: When WAL failover is configured, the
254: 	// Pebble commit pipeline may retain a pointer to the batch.data beyond the
255: 	// return of [Batch.Commit]. The user of the Batch may commit their batch
256: 	// and call Close or Reset before the commit pipeline is finished reading
257: 	// the data slice. Recycling immediately would cause a data race.
258: 	//
259: 	// To resolve this data race, this [lifecycle] atomic is used to determine
260: 	// safety and responsibility of reusing a batch. The low bits of the atomic
261: 	// are used as a reference count (really just the lowest bit—in practice
262: 	// there's only 1 code path that references). The [Batch] is passed into
263: 	// [wal.Writer]'s WriteRecord method as a [RefCount] implementation. The
264: 	// wal.Writer guarantees that if it will read [Batch.data] after the call to
265: 	// WriteRecord returns, it will increment the reference count. When it's
266: 	// complete, it'll unreference through invoking [Batch.Unref].
267: 	//
268: 	// When the committer of a batch indicates intent to recycle a Batch through
269: 	// calling [Batch.Reset] or [Batch.Close], the lifecycle atomic is read. If
270: 	// an outstanding reference remains, it's unsafe to reuse Batch.data yet. In
271: 	// [Batch.Reset] the caller wants to reuse the [Batch] immediately, so we
272: 	// discard b.data to recycle the struct but not the underlying byte slice.
273: 	// In [Batch.Close], we set a special high bit [batchClosedBit] on lifecycle
274: 	// that indicates that the user will not use [Batch] again and we're free to
275: 	// recycle it when safe. When the commit pipeline eventually calls
276: 	// [Batch.Unref], the [batchClosedBit] is noticed and the batch is
277: 	// recycled.
278: 	lifecycle atomic.Int32
279: }
280: 
281: // batchClosedBit is a bit stored on Batch.lifecycle to indicate that the user
282: // called [Batch.Close] to release a Batch, but an open reference count
283: // prevented immediate recycling.
284: const batchClosedBit = 1 << 30
285: 
286: // TODO(jackson): Hide the wal.RefCount implementation from the public Batch interface.
287: 
288: // Ref implements wal.RefCount. If the WAL writer may need to read b.data after
289: // it returns, it invokes Ref to increment the lifecycle's reference count. When
290: // it's finished, it invokes Unref.
291: func (b *Batch) Ref() {
292: 	b.lifecycle.Add(+1)
293: }
294: 
295: // Unref implemets wal.RefCount.
296: func (b *Batch) Unref() {
297: 	if v := b.lifecycle.Add(-1); (v ^ batchClosedBit) == 0 {
298: 		// The [batchClosedBit] high bit is set, and there are no outstanding
299: 		// references. The user of the Batch called [Batch.Close], expecting the
300: 		// batch to be recycled. However, our outstanding reference count
301: 		// prevented recycling. As the last to dereference, we're now
302: 		// responsible for releasing the batch.
303: 		b.lifecycle.Store(0)
304: 		b.release()
305: 	}
306: }
307: 
308: // batchInternal contains the set of fields within Batch that are non-atomic and
309: // capable of being reset using a *b = batchInternal{} struct copy.
310: type batchInternal struct {
311: 	// Data is the wire format of a batch's log entry:
312: 	//   - 8 bytes for a sequence number of the first batch element,
313: 	//     or zeroes if the batch has not yet been applied,
314: 	//   - 4 bytes for the count: the number of elements in the batch,
315: 	//     or "\xff\xff\xff\xff" if the batch is invalid,
316: 	//   - count elements, being:
317: 	//     - one byte for the kind
318: 	//     - the varint-string user key,
319: 	//     - the varint-string value (if kind != delete).
320: 	// The sequence number and count are stored in little-endian order.
321: 	//
322: 	// The data field can be (but is not guaranteed to be) nil for new
323: 	// batches. Large batches will set the data field to nil when committed as
324: 	// the data has been moved to a flushableBatch and inserted into the queue of
325: 	// memtables.
326: 	data     []byte
327: 	comparer *base.Comparer
328: 	opts     batchOptions
329: 
330: 	// An upper bound on required space to add this batch to a memtable.
331: 	// Note that although batches are limited to 4 GiB in size, that limit
332: 	// applies to len(data), not the memtable size. The upper bound on the
333: 	// size of a memtable node is larger than the overhead of the batch's log
334: 	// encoding, so memTableSize is larger than len(data) and may overflow a
335: 	// uint32.
336: 	memTableSize uint64
337: 
338: 	// The db to which the batch will be committed. Do not change this field
339: 	// after the batch has been created as it might invalidate internal state.
340: 	// Batch.memTableSize is only refreshed if Batch.db is set. Setting db to
341: 	// nil once it has been set implies that the Batch has encountered an error.
342: 	db *DB
343: 
344: 	// The count of records in the batch. This count will be stored in the batch
345: 	// data whenever Repr() is called.
346: 	count uint64
347: 
348: 	// The count of range deletions in the batch. Updated every time a range
349: 	// deletion is added.
350: 	countRangeDels uint64
351: 
352: 	// The count of range key sets, unsets and deletes in the batch. Updated
353: 	// every time a RANGEKEYSET, RANGEKEYUNSET or RANGEKEYDEL key is added.
354: 	countRangeKeys uint64
355: 
356: 	// A deferredOp struct, stored in the Batch so that a pointer can be returned
357: 	// from the *Deferred() methods rather than a value.
358: 	deferredOp DeferredBatchOp
359: 
360: 	// An optional skiplist keyed by offset into data of the entry.
361: 	index         *batchskl.Skiplist
362: 	rangeDelIndex *batchskl.Skiplist
363: 	rangeKeyIndex *batchskl.Skiplist
364: 
365: 	// Fragmented range deletion tombstones. Cached the first time a range
366: 	// deletion iterator is requested. The cache is invalidated whenever a new
367: 	// range deletion is added to the batch. This cache can only be used when
368: 	// opening an iterator to read at a batch sequence number >=
369: 	// tombstonesSeqNum. This is the case for all new iterators created over a
370: 	// batch but it's not the case for all cloned iterators.
371: 	tombstones       []keyspan.Span
372: 	tombstonesSeqNum base.SeqNum
373: 
374: 	// Fragmented range key spans. Cached the first time a range key iterator is
375: 	// requested. The cache is invalidated whenever a new range key
376: 	// (RangeKey{Set,Unset,Del}) is added to the batch. This cache can only be
377: 	// used when opening an iterator to read at a batch sequence number >=
378: 	// rangeKeysSeqNum. This is the case for all new iterators created over a
379: 	// batch but it's not the case for all cloned iterators.
380: 	rangeKeys       []keyspan.Span
381: 	rangeKeysSeqNum base.SeqNum
382: 
383: 	// The flushableBatch wrapper if the batch is too large to fit in the
384: 	// memtable.
385: 	flushable *flushableBatch
386: 
387: 	// minimumFormatMajorVersion indicates the format major version required in
388: 	// order to commit this batch. If an operation requires a particular format
389: 	// major version, it ratchets the batch's minimumFormatMajorVersion. When
390: 	// the batch is committed, this is validated against the database's current
391: 	// format major version.
392: 	minimumFormatMajorVersion FormatMajorVersion
393: 
394: 	// Synchronous Apply uses the commit WaitGroup for both publishing the
395: 	// seqnum and waiting for the WAL fsync (if needed). Asynchronous
396: 	// ApplyNoSyncWait, which implies WriteOptions.Sync is true, uses the commit
397: 	// WaitGroup for publishing the seqnum and the fsyncWait WaitGroup for
398: 	// waiting for the WAL fsync.
399: 	//
400: 	// TODO(sumeer): if we find that ApplyNoSyncWait in conjunction with
401: 	// SyncWait is causing higher memory usage because of the time duration
402: 	// between when the sync is already done, and a goroutine calls SyncWait
403: 	// (followed by Batch.Close), we could separate out {fsyncWait, commitErr}
404: 	// into a separate struct that is allocated separately (using another
405: 	// sync.Pool), and only that struct needs to outlive Batch.Close (which
406: 	// could then be called immediately after ApplyNoSyncWait). commitStats
407: 	// will also need to be in this separate struct.
408: 	commit    sync.WaitGroup
409: 	fsyncWait sync.WaitGroup
410: 
411: 	commitStats BatchCommitStats
412: 
413: 	commitErr error
414: 
415: 	// Position bools together to reduce the sizeof the struct.
416: 
417: 	// ingestedSSTBatch indicates that the batch contains one or more key kinds
418: 	// of InternalKeyKindIngestSST, InternalKeyKindIngestSSTWithBlobs, or
419: 	// InternalKeyKindExcise. If the batch contains key kinds of IngestSST*/Excise
420: 	// then it will only contain key kinds of IngestSST/Excise.
421: 	ingestedSSTBatch bool
422: 
423: 	// committing is set to true when a batch begins to commit. It's used to
424: 	// ensure the batch is not mutated concurrently. It is not an atomic
425: 	// deliberately, so as to avoid the overhead on batch mutations. This is
426: 	// okay, because under correct usage this field will never be accessed
427: 	// concurrently. It's only under incorrect usage the memory accesses of this
428: 	// variable may violate memory safety. Since we don't use atomics here,
429: 	// false negatives are possible.
430: 	committing bool
431: }
432: 
433: // BatchCommitStats exposes stats related to committing a batch.
434: //
435: // NB: there is no Pebble internal tracing (using LoggerAndTracer) of slow
436: // batch commits. The caller can use these stats to do their own tracing as
437: // needed.
438: type BatchCommitStats struct {
439: 	// TotalDuration is the time spent in DB.{Apply,ApplyNoSyncWait} or
440: 	// Batch.Commit, plus the time waiting in Batch.SyncWait. If there is a gap
441: 	// between calling ApplyNoSyncWait and calling SyncWait, that gap could
442: 	// include some duration in which real work was being done for the commit
443: 	// and will not be included here. This missing time is considered acceptable
444: 	// since the goal of these stats is to understand user-facing latency.
445: 	//
446: 	// TotalDuration includes time spent in various queues both inside Pebble
447: 	// and outside Pebble (I/O queues, goroutine scheduler queue, mutex wait
448: 	// etc.). For some of these queues (which we consider important) the wait
449: 	// times are included below -- these expose low-level implementation detail
450: 	// and are meant for expert diagnosis and subject to change. There may be
451: 	// unaccounted time after subtracting those values from TotalDuration.
452: 	TotalDuration time.Duration
453: 	// SemaphoreWaitDuration is the wait time for semaphores in
454: 	// commitPipeline.Commit.
455: 	SemaphoreWaitDuration time.Duration
456: 	// WALQueueWaitDuration is the wait time for allocating memory blocks in the
457: 	// LogWriter (due to the LogWriter not writing fast enough). At the moment
458: 	// this is duration is always zero because a single WAL will allow
459: 	// allocating memory blocks up to the entire memtable size. In the future,
460: 	// we may pipeline WALs and bound the WAL queued blocks separately, so this
461: 	// field is preserved for that possibility.
462: 	WALQueueWaitDuration time.Duration
463: 	// MemTableWriteStallDuration is the wait caused by a write stall due to too
464: 	// many memtables (due to not flushing fast enough).
465: 	MemTableWriteStallDuration time.Duration
466: 	// L0ReadAmpWriteStallDuration is the wait caused by a write stall due to
467: 	// high read amplification in L0 (due to not compacting fast enough out of
468: 	// L0).
469: 	L0ReadAmpWriteStallDuration time.Duration
470: 	// WALRotationDuration is the wait time for WAL rotation, which includes
471: 	// syncing and closing the old WAL and creating (or reusing) a new one.
472: 	WALRotationDuration time.Duration
473: 	// CommitWaitDuration is the wait for publishing the seqnum plus the
474: 	// duration for the WAL sync (if requested). The former should be tiny and
475: 	// one can assume that this is all due to the WAL sync.
476: 	CommitWaitDuration time.Duration
477: }

535: // nextSeqNum returns the batch "sequence number" that will be given to the next
536: // key written to the batch. During iteration keys within an indexed batch are
537: // given a sequence number consisting of their offset within the batch combined

545: func (b *Batch) release() {
546: 	if b.db == nil {
547: 		// The batch was not created using newBatch or newIndexedBatch, or an error
548: 		// was encountered. We don't try to reuse batches that encountered an error
549: 		// because they might be stuck somewhere in the system and attempting to
550: 		// reuse such batches is a recipe for onerous debugging sessions. Instead,
551: 		// let the GC do its job.
552: 		return
553: 	}
554: 	b.db = nil
555: 
556: 	// NB: This is ugly (it would be cleaner if we could just assign a Batch{}),
557: 	// but necessary so that we can use atomic.StoreUint32 for the Batch.applied
558: 	// field. Without using an atomic to clear that field the Go race detector
559: 	// complains.
560: 	b.reset()
561: 	b.comparer = nil
562: 
563: 	if b.index == nil {
564: 		batchPool.Put(b)
565: 	} else {
566: 		b.index, b.rangeDelIndex, b.rangeKeyIndex = nil, nil, nil
567: 		indexedBatchPool.Put((*indexedBatch)(unsafe.Pointer(b)))
568: 	}
569: }

571: func (b *Batch) refreshMemTableSize() error {
572: 	b.memTableSize = 0
573: 	if len(b.data) < batchrepr.HeaderLen {
574: 		return nil
575: 	}
576: 
577: 	b.countRangeDels = 0
578: 	b.countRangeKeys = 0
579: 	b.minimumFormatMajorVersion = 0
580: 	for r := b.Reader(); ; {
581: 		kind, key, value, ok, err := r.Next()
582: 		if !ok {
583: 			if err != nil {
584: 				return err
585: 			}
586: 			break
587: 		}
588: 		if kind > InternalKeyKindMax {
589: 			// Note In some circumstances this might be temporary memory
590: 			// corruption that can be recovered by discarding the batch and
591: 			// trying again. In other cases, the batch repr might've been
592: 			// already persisted elsewhere, and we'll loop continuously trying
593: 			// to commit the same corrupted batch. The caller is responsible for
594: 			// distinguishing.
595: 			return errors.Wrapf(ErrInvalidBatch, "unrecognized kind %v", kind)
596: 		}
597: 		info := batchKinds[kind]
598: 		b.minimumFormatMajorVersion = max(b.minimumFormatMajorVersion, info.minFMV)
599: 		switch info.category {
600: 		case batchKindPoint:
601: 			// Contributes to memtable size below.
602: 		case batchKindRangeDel:
603: 			b.countRangeDels++
604: 		case batchKindRangeKey:
605: 			b.countRangeKeys++
606: 		case batchKindLogData, batchKindIngestOrExcise:
607: 			// These kinds do not contribute to memtable size.
608: 			continue
609: 		default: // batchKindInvalid
610: 			return errors.Wrapf(ErrInvalidBatch, "unrecognized kind %v", kind)
611: 		}
612: 		b.memTableSize += memTableEntrySize(len(key), len(value))
613: 	}
614: 	return nil
615: }

617: // Apply the operations contained in the batch to the receiver batch.
618: //
619: // It is safe to modify the contents of the arguments after Apply returns.
620: //
621: // Apply returns ErrInvalidBatch if the provided batch is invalid in any way.
622: func (b *Batch) Apply(batch *Batch, _ *WriteOptions) error {
623: 	if b.ingestedSSTBatch {
624: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: invalid batch application"))
625: 	}
626: 	if len(batch.data) == 0 {
627: 		return nil
628: 	}
629: 	if len(batch.data) < batchrepr.HeaderLen {
630: 		return ErrInvalidBatch
631: 	}
632: 
633: 	offset := len(b.data)
634: 	if offset == 0 {
635: 		b.init(offset)
636: 		offset = batchrepr.HeaderLen
637: 	}
638: 	b.data = append(b.data, batch.data[batchrepr.HeaderLen:]...)
639: 
640: 	b.setCount(b.Count() + batch.Count())
641: 	b.minimumFormatMajorVersion = max(b.minimumFormatMajorVersion, batch.minimumFormatMajorVersion)
642: 
643: 	if b.db != nil || b.index != nil {
644: 		// Only iterate over the new entries if we need to track memTableSize or in
645: 		// order to update the index.
646: 		for iter := batchrepr.Reader(b.data[offset:]); len(iter) > 0; {
647: 			offset := uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&iter[0])) - uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&b.data[0]))
648: 			kind, key, value, ok, err := iter.Next()
649: 			if !ok {
650: 				if err != nil {
651: 					return err
652: 				}
653: 				break
654: 			}
655: 			if kind > InternalKeyKindMax {
656: 				// Note In some circumstances this might be temporary memory
657: 				// corruption that can be recovered by discarding the batch and
658: 				// trying again. In other cases, the batch repr might've been
659: 				// already persisted elsewhere, and we'll loop continuously
660: 				// trying to commit the same corrupted batch. The caller is
661: 				// responsible for distinguishing.
662: 				return errors.Wrapf(ErrInvalidBatch, "unrecognized kind %v", kind)
663: 			}
664: 			info := batchKinds[kind]
665: 			// Ratchet the receiver's minimumFormatMajorVersion from the record's
666: 			// kind. Not all paths that populate a batch set
667: 			// minimumFormatMajorVersion (e.g. SetRepr on a batch with a nil db
668: 			// skips refreshMemTableSize); so, the source batch's value may be
669: 			// stale.
670: 			b.minimumFormatMajorVersion = max(b.minimumFormatMajorVersion, info.minFMV)
671: 			switch info.category {
672: 			case batchKindPoint:
673: 				// Contributes to index/memtable size below.
674: 			case batchKindRangeDel:
675: 				b.countRangeDels++
676: 			case batchKindRangeKey:
677: 				b.countRangeKeys++
678: 			case batchKindLogData:
679: 				// LogData does not contribute to memtable size.
680: 				continue
681: 			case batchKindIngestOrExcise:
682: 				panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: invalid key kind for batch.Apply: %s", kind))
683: 			default: // batchKindInvalid
684: 				return errors.Wrapf(ErrInvalidBatch, "unrecognized kind %v", kind)
685: 			}
686: 			if b.index != nil {
687: 				var err error
688: 				switch info.category {
689: 				case batchKindRangeDel:
690: 					b.tombstones = nil
691: 					b.tombstonesSeqNum = 0
692: 					if b.rangeDelIndex == nil {
693: 						b.rangeDelIndex = batchskl.NewSkiplist(&b.data, b.comparer.Compare, b.comparer.AbbreviatedKey)
694: 					}
695: 					err = b.rangeDelIndex.Add(uint32(offset))
696: 				case batchKindRangeKey:
697: 					b.rangeKeys = nil
698: 					b.rangeKeysSeqNum = 0
699: 					if b.rangeKeyIndex == nil {
700: 						b.rangeKeyIndex = batchskl.NewSkiplist(&b.data, b.comparer.Compare, b.comparer.AbbreviatedKey)
701: 					}
702: 					err = b.rangeKeyIndex.Add(uint32(offset))
703: 				default:
704: 					err = b.index.Add(uint32(offset))
705: 				}
706: 				if err != nil {
707: 					return err
708: 				}
709: 			}
710: 			b.memTableSize += memTableEntrySize(len(key), len(value))
711: 		}
712: 	}
713: 	return nil
714: }

716: // Get gets the value for the given key. It returns ErrNotFound if the Batch
717: // does not contain the key.
718: //
719: // The caller should not modify the contents of the returned slice, but it is
720: // safe to modify the contents of the argument after Get returns. The returned
721: // slice will remain valid until the returned Closer is closed. On success, the
722: // caller MUST call closer.Close() or a memory leak will occur.

724: 	if b.index == nil {
725: 		return nil, nil, ErrNotIndexed
726: 	}
727: 	return b.db.getInternal(key, b, nil /* snapshot */)

730: func (b *Batch) prepareDeferredKeyValueRecord(keyLen, valueLen int, kind InternalKeyKind) {
731: 	if b.committing {
732: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: batch already committing"))
733: 	}
734: 	if len(b.data) == 0 {
735: 		b.init(keyLen + valueLen + 2*binary.MaxVarintLen64 + batchrepr.HeaderLen)
736: 	}
737: 	b.count++
738: 	b.memTableSize += memTableEntrySize(keyLen, valueLen)
739: 	b.minimumFormatMajorVersion = max(b.minimumFormatMajorVersion, batchKinds[kind].minFMV)
740: 
741: 	pos := len(b.data)
742: 	b.deferredOp.offset = uint32(pos)
743: 	b.grow(1 + 2*maxVarintLen32 + keyLen + valueLen)
744: 	b.data[pos] = byte(kind)
745: 	pos++
746: 
747: 	{
748: 		// TODO(peter): Manually inlined version binary.PutUvarint(). This is 20%
749: 		// faster on BenchmarkBatchSet on go1.13. Remove if go1.14 or future
750: 		// versions show this to not be a performance win.
751: 		x := uint32(keyLen)
752: 		for x >= 0x80 {
753: 			b.data[pos] = byte(x) | 0x80
754: 			x >>= 7
755: 			pos++
756: 		}
757: 		b.data[pos] = byte(x)
758: 		pos++
759: 	}
760: 
761: 	b.deferredOp.Key = b.data[pos : pos+keyLen]
762: 	pos += keyLen
763: 
764: 	{
765: 		// TODO(peter): Manually inlined version binary.PutUvarint(). This is 20%
766: 		// faster on BenchmarkBatchSet on go1.13. Remove if go1.14 or future
767: 		// versions show this to not be a performance win.
768: 		x := uint32(valueLen)
769: 		for x >= 0x80 {
770: 			b.data[pos] = byte(x) | 0x80
771: 			x >>= 7
772: 			pos++
773: 		}
774: 		b.data[pos] = byte(x)
775: 		pos++
776: 	}
777: 
778: 	b.deferredOp.Value = b.data[pos : pos+valueLen]
779: 	// Shrink data since varints may be shorter than the upper bound.
780: 	b.data = b.data[:pos+valueLen]
781: }

821: // AddInternalKey allows the caller to add an internal key of point key or range
822: // key kinds (but not RangeDelete) to a batch. Passing in an internal key of
823: // kind RangeDelete will result in a panic. Note that the seqnum in the internal
824: // key is effectively ignored, even though the Kind is preserved. This is
825: // because the batch format does not allow for a per-key seqnum to be specified,
826: // only a batch-wide one.

829: // supported with this method as they require specialized logic.

831: 	keyLen := len(key.UserKey)
832: 	hasValue := false
833: 	switch kind := key.Kind(); kind {
834: 	case InternalKeyKindRangeDelete:
835: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("unexpected range delete in AddInternalKey"))
836: 	case InternalKeyKindSingleDelete, InternalKeyKindDelete:
837: 		b.prepareDeferredKeyRecord(keyLen, kind)
838: 		b.deferredOp.index = b.index
839: 	case InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet, InternalKeyKindRangeKeyUnset, InternalKeyKindRangeKeyDelete:
840: 		b.prepareDeferredKeyValueRecord(keyLen, len(value), kind)

842: 		b.incrementRangeKeysCount()
843: 	default:
844: 		b.prepareDeferredKeyValueRecord(keyLen, len(value), kind)
845: 		hasValue = true
846: 		b.deferredOp.index = b.index
847: 	}
848: 	copy(b.deferredOp.Key, key.UserKey)
849: 	if hasValue {
850: 		copy(b.deferredOp.Value, value)
851: 	}
852: 
853: 	// TODO(peter): Manually inline DeferredBatchOp.Finish(). Mid-stack inlining
854: 	// in go1.13 will remove the need for this.
855: 	if b.index != nil {
856: 		if err := b.index.Add(b.deferredOp.offset); err != nil {
857: 			return err
858: 		}
859: 	}
860: 	return nil
861: }

230: // DB provides a concurrent, persistent ordered key/value store.
231: //
232: // A DB's basic operations (Get, Set, Delete) should be self-explanatory. Get
233: // and Delete will return ErrNotFound if the requested key is not in the store.
234: // Callers are free to ignore this error.
235: //
236: // A DB also allows for iterating over the key/value pairs in key order. If d
237: // is a DB, the code below prints all key/value pairs whose keys are 'greater
238: // than or equal to' k:
239: //
240: //	iter := d.NewIter(readOptions)
241: //	for iter.SeekGE(k); iter.Valid(); iter.Next() {
242: //		fmt.Printf("key=%q value=%q\n", iter.Key(), iter.Value())
243: //	}
244: //	return iter.Close()
245: //
246: // The Options struct holds the optional parameters for the DB, including a
247: // Comparer to define a 'less than' relationship over keys. It is always valid
248: // to pass a nil *Options, which means to use the default parameter values. Any
249: // zero field of a non-nil *Options also means to use the default value for
250: // that parameter. Thus, the code below uses a custom Comparer, but the default
251: // values for every other parameter:
252: //
253: //	db := pebble.Open(&Options{
254: //		Comparer: myComparer,
255: //	})

573: // RecordSeparatedValueRetrievals begins collection of stack traces that are
574: // retrieving separated values. If a profile has already begun, an error is
575: // returned. If successful, the stop function must be called to stop the
576: // collection and return the resulting profile.

582: 	swapped := d.valueRetrievalProfile.CompareAndSwap(nil, p)

586: 	return func() *metrics.ValueRetrievalProfile {
587: 		if !d.valueRetrievalProfile.CompareAndSwap(p, nil) {
588: 			panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("profile already stopped"))

736: 	// Only release the batch on success.
737: 	return b.Close()
738: }

740: // RangeKeyDelete deletes all of the range keys in the range [start,end)
741: // (inclusive on start, exclusive on end). It does not delete point keys (for
742: // that use DeleteRange). RangeKeyDelete removes all range keys within the
743: // bounds, including those with or without suffixes.
744: //
745: // It is safe to modify the contents of the arguments after RangeKeyDelete
746: // returns.
747: func (d *DB) RangeKeyDelete(start, end []byte, opts *WriteOptions) error {
748: 	b := newBatch(d)
749: 	_ = b.RangeKeyDelete(start, end, opts)
750: 	if err := d.Apply(b, opts); err != nil {
751: 		return err
752: 	}
753: 	// Only release the batch on success.
754: 	return b.Close()
755: }

757: // Apply the operations contained in the batch to the DB. If the batch is large
758: // the contents of the batch may be retained by the database. If that occurs
759: // the batch contents will be cleared preventing the caller from attempting to
760: // reuse them.
761: //
762: // It is safe to modify the contents of the arguments after Apply returns.
763: //
764: // Apply returns ErrInvalidBatch if the provided batch is invalid in any way.
765: func (d *DB) Apply(batch *Batch, opts *WriteOptions) error {
766: 	return d.applyInternal(batch, opts, false)
767: }
768: 
769: // ApplyNoSyncWait must only be used when opts.Sync is true and the caller
770: // does not want to wait for the WAL fsync to happen. The method will return
771: // once the mutation is applied to the memtable and is visible (note that a
772: // mutation is visible before the WAL sync even in the wait case, so we have
773: // not weakened the durability semantics). The caller must call Batch.SyncWait
774: // to wait for the WAL fsync. The caller must not Close the batch without
775: // first calling Batch.SyncWait.
776: //
777: // RECOMMENDATION: Prefer using Apply unless you really understand why you
778: // need ApplyNoSyncWait.
779: // EXPERIMENTAL: API/feature subject to change. Do not yet use outside
780: // CockroachDB.
781: func (d *DB) ApplyNoSyncWait(batch *Batch, opts *WriteOptions) error {
782: 	if !opts.GetSync() {
783: 		return errors.Errorf("cannot request asynchronous apply when WriteOptions.Sync is false")
784: 	}
785: 	return d.applyInternal(batch, opts, true)
786: }

788: // REQUIRES: noSyncWait => opts.Sync
789: func (d *DB) applyInternal(batch *Batch, opts *WriteOptions, noSyncWait bool) error {
790: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
791: 		panic(err)
792: 	}
793: 	if batch.committing {
794: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: batch already committing"))
795: 	}
796: 	if batch.applied.Load() {
797: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: batch already applied"))
798: 	}
799: 	if d.opts.ReadOnly {
800: 		return ErrReadOnly
801: 	}
802: 	if batch.db != nil && batch.db != d {
803: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: batch db mismatch: %p != %p", errors.Safe(batch.db), errors.Safe(d)))
804: 	}
805: 
806: 	sync := opts.GetSync()
807: 	if sync && d.opts.DisableWAL {
808: 		return errors.New("pebble: WAL disabled")
809: 	}
810: 
811: 	if fmv := d.FormatMajorVersion(); fmv < batch.minimumFormatMajorVersion {
812: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf(
813: 			"pebble: batch requires at least format major version %d (current: %d)",
814: 			batch.minimumFormatMajorVersion, fmv,
815: 		))
816: 	}
817: 
818: 	if batch.countRangeKeys > 0 {
819: 		if d.split == nil {
820: 			return errNoSplit
821: 		}
822: 	}
823: 	batch.committing = true
824: 
825: 	if batch.db == nil {
826: 		if err := batch.refreshMemTableSize(); err != nil {
827: 			return err
828: 		}
829: 	}
830: 	if batch.memTableSize >= d.largeBatchThreshold {
831: 		var err error
832: 		batch.flushable, err = newFlushableBatch(batch, d.opts.Comparer)
833: 		if err != nil {
834: 			return err
835: 		}
836: 	}
837: 	if err := d.commit.Commit(batch, sync, noSyncWait); err != nil {
838: 		// There isn't much we can do on an error here. The commit pipeline will be
839: 		// horked at this point.
840: 		d.opts.Logger.Fatalf("pebble: fatal commit error: %v", err)
841: 	}
842: 	// If this is a large batch, we need to clear the batch contents as the
843: 	// flushable batch may still be present in the flushables queue.
844: 	//
845: 	// TODO(peter): Currently large batches are written to the WAL. We could
846: 	// skip the WAL write and instead wait for the large batch to be flushed to
847: 	// an sstable. For a 100 MB batch, this might actually be faster. For a 1
848: 	// GB batch this is almost certainly faster.
849: 	if batch.flushable != nil {
850: 		batch.data = nil
851: 	}
852: 	return nil
853: }

855: func (d *DB) commitApply(b *Batch, mem *memTable) error {
856: 	if b.flushable != nil {
857: 		// This is a large batch which was already added to the immutable queue.
858: 		return nil
859: 	}
860: 	err := mem.apply(b, b.SeqNum())
861: 	if err != nil {
862: 		return err
863: 	}
864: 
865: 	// If the batch contains range tombstones and the database is configured
866: 	// to flush range deletions, schedule a delayed flush so that disk space
867: 	// may be reclaimed without additional writes or an explicit flush.
868: 	if b.countRangeDels > 0 && d.opts.FlushDelayDeleteRange > 0 {
869: 		d.mu.Lock()
870: 		d.maybeScheduleDelayedFlush(mem, d.opts.FlushDelayDeleteRange)
871: 		d.mu.Unlock()
872: 	}
873: 
874: 	// If the batch contains range keys and the database is configured to flush
875: 	// range keys, schedule a delayed flush so that the range keys are cleared
876: 	// from the memtable.
877: 	if b.countRangeKeys > 0 && d.opts.FlushDelayRangeKey > 0 {
878: 		d.mu.Lock()
879: 		d.maybeScheduleDelayedFlush(mem, d.opts.FlushDelayRangeKey)
880: 		d.mu.Unlock()
881: 	}
882: 
883: 	if mem.writerUnref() {
884: 		d.mu.Lock()
885: 		d.maybeScheduleFlush()
886: 		d.mu.Unlock()
887: 	}
888: 	return nil
889: }

891: func (d *DB) commitWrite(b *Batch, syncWG *sync.WaitGroup, syncErr *error) (*memTable, error) {
892: 	var size int64
893: 	repr := b.Repr()
894: 
895: 	if b.flushable != nil {
896: 		// We have a large batch. Such batches are special in that they don't get
897: 		// added to the memtable, and are instead inserted into the queue of
898: 		// memtables. The call to makeRoomForWrite with this batch will force the
899: 		// current memtable to be flushed. We want the large batch to be part of
900: 		// the same log, so we add it to the WAL here, rather than after the call
901: 		// to makeRoomForWrite().
902: 		//
903: 		// Set the sequence number since it was not set to the correct value earlier
904: 		// (see comment in newFlushableBatch()).
905: 		b.flushable.setSeqNum(b.SeqNum())
906: 		if !d.opts.DisableWAL {
907: 			var err error
908: 			size, err = d.mu.log.writer.WriteRecord(repr, wal.SyncOptions{Done: syncWG, Err: syncErr}, b)
909: 			if err != nil {
910: 				panic(err)
911: 			}
912: 		}
913: 	}
914: 
915: 	var err error
916: 	// Grab a reference to the memtable. We don't hold DB.mu, but we do hold
917: 	// d.commit.mu. It's okay for readers of d.mu.mem.mutable to only hold one of
918: 	// d.commit.mu or d.mu, because memtable rotations require holding both.
919: 	mem := d.mu.mem.mutable
920: 	// Batches which contain keys of kind InternalKeyKindIngestSST or InternalKeyKindIngestSSTWithBlobs will
921: 	// never be applied to the memtable, so we don't need to make room for
922: 	// write.
923: 	if !b.ingestedSSTBatch {
924: 		// Flushable batches will require a rotation of the memtable regardless,
925: 		// so only attempt an optimistic reservation of space in the current
926: 		// memtable if this batch is not a large flushable batch.
927: 		if b.flushable == nil {
928: 			err = d.mu.mem.mutable.prepare(b)
929: 		}
930: 		if b.flushable != nil || err == arenaskl.ErrArenaFull {
931: 			// Slow path.
932: 			// We need to acquire DB.mu and rotate the memtable.
933: 			func() {
934: 				d.mu.Lock()
935: 				defer d.mu.Unlock()
936: 				err = d.makeRoomForWrite(b)
937: 				mem = d.mu.mem.mutable
938: 			}()
939: 		}
940: 	}
941: 	if err != nil {
942: 		return nil, err
943: 	}
944: 	if d.opts.DisableWAL {
945: 		return mem, nil
946: 	}
947: 	d.logBytesIn.Add(uint64(len(repr)))
948: 
949: 	if b.flushable == nil {
950: 		size, err = d.mu.log.writer.WriteRecord(repr, wal.SyncOptions{Done: syncWG, Err: syncErr}, b)
951: 		if err != nil {
952: 			panic(err)
953: 		}
954: 	}
955: 
956: 	d.logSize.Store(uint64(size))
957: 	return mem, err
958: }

960: // iterAllocCommon contains the iterator-allocation state shared between the
961: // V1 (iterAlloc) and V2 (iterV2Alloc) pool entries.
962: type iterAllocCommon struct {
963: 	keyBuf              []byte    `invariants:"reused"`
964: 	boundsBuf           [2][]byte `invariants:"reused"`
965: 	prefixOrFullSeekKey []byte    `invariants:"reused"`

970: type iterAlloc struct {
971: 	iterAllocCommon

978: // assertZeroed asserts that i is a "zeroed" value. See assertZeroed for the
979: // definition of "zeroed". It's used to ensure we're properly zeroing out memory
980: // before returning the iterAlloc to the shared pool.
981: func (i *iterAlloc) assertZeroed() {
982: 	v := reflect.ValueOf(i).Elem()
983: 	if err := assertZeroed(v); err != nil {
984: 		panic(err)
985: 	}
986: }
987: 
988: // assertZeroed asserts that v is a "zeroed" value. A "zeroed" value is a value
989: // that is:
990: //   - the Go zero value for its type, or
991: //   - a pointer to a "zeroed" value, or
992: //   - a slice of len()=0, with any values in the backing array being "zeroed
993: //     values", or
994: //   - a struct with all fields being "zeroed" values,
995: //   - a struct field explicitly marked with a "invariants:reused" tag.
996: func assertZeroed(v reflect.Value) error {
997: 	if v.IsZero() {
998: 		return nil
999: 	}
1000: 	typ := v.Type()
1001: 	switch typ.Kind() {
1002: 	case reflect.Pointer:
1003: 		return assertZeroed(v.Elem())
1004: 	case reflect.Slice:
1005: 		if v.Len() > 0 {
1006: 			return errors.AssertionFailedf("%s is not zeroed (%d len): %#v", errors.Safe(typ.Name()), errors.Safe(v.Len()), v)
1007: 		}
1008: 		resliced := v.Slice(0, v.Cap())
1009: 		for i := 0; i < resliced.Len(); i++ {
1010: 			if err := assertZeroed(resliced.Index(i)); err != nil {
1011: 				return errors.Wrapf(err, "[%d]", i)
1012: 			}
1013: 		}
1014: 		return nil
1015: 	case reflect.Struct:
1016: 		for i := 0; i < typ.NumField(); i++ {
1017: 			if typ.Field(i).Tag.Get("invariants") == "reused" {
1018: 				continue
1019: 			}
1020: 			if err := assertZeroed(v.Field(i)); err != nil {
1021: 				return errors.Wrapf(err, "%q", typ.Field(i).Name)
1022: 			}
1023: 		}
1024: 		return nil
1025: 	}
1026: 	return errors.AssertionFailedf("%s (%s) is not zeroed: %#v", errors.Safe(typ.Name()), typ.Kind(), v)
1027: }

1076: // snapshotIterOpts denotes snapshot-related iterator options when calling
1077: // newIter. These are the possible cases for a snapshotIterOpts:
1078: //   - No snapshot: All fields are zero values.
1079: //   - Classic snapshot: Only `seqNum` is set. The latest readState will be used
1080: //     and the specified seqNum will be used as the snapshot seqNum.
1081: //   - EventuallyFileOnlySnapshot (EFOS) behaving as a classic snapshot. Only
1082: //     the `seqNum` is set. The latest readState will be used
1083: //     and the specified seqNum will be used as the snapshot seqNum.
1084: //   - EFOS in file-only state: Only `seqNum` and `vers` are set. All the
1085: //     relevant SSTs are referenced by the *version.
1086: //   - EFOS that has been excised but is in alwaysCreateIters mode (tests only).
1087: //     Only `seqNum` and `readState` are set.
1088: type snapshotIterOpts struct {
1089: 	seqNum    base.SeqNum
1090: 	vers      *manifest.Version
1091: 	readState *readState
1092: }

1094: type batchIterOpts struct {
1095: 	batchOnly bool
1096: }

1102: // newIter constructs a new iterator, merging in batch iterators as an extra
1103: // level.
1104: func (d *DB) newIter(
1105: 	ctx context.Context, batch *Batch, newIterOpts newIterOpts, o *IterOptions,
1106: ) *Iterator {
1107: 	if newIterOpts.batch.batchOnly {
1108: 		if batch == nil {
1109: 			panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("batchOnly is true, but batch is nil"))
1110: 		}
1111: 		if newIterOpts.snapshot.vers != nil {
1112: 			panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("batchOnly is true, but snapshotIterOpts is initialized"))
1113: 		}
1114: 	}
1115: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1116: 		panic(err)
1117: 	}
1118: 	seqNum := newIterOpts.snapshot.seqNum
1119: 	if o != nil && o.RangeKeyMasking.Suffix != nil && o.KeyTypes != IterKeyTypePointsAndRanges {
1120: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: range key masking requires IterKeyTypePointsAndRanges"))
1121: 	}
1122: 	if (batch != nil || seqNum != 0) && (o != nil && o.OnlyReadGuaranteedDurable) {
1123: 		// We could add support for OnlyReadGuaranteedDurable on snapshots if
1124: 		// there was a need: this would require checking that the sequence number
1125: 		// of the snapshot has been flushed, by comparing with
1126: 		// DB.mem.queue[0].logSeqNum.
1127: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("OnlyReadGuaranteedDurable is not supported for batches or snapshots"))
1128: 	}
1129: 	var readState *readState
1130: 	var newIters tableNewIters
1131: 	var newIterRangeKey keyspanimpl.TableNewSpanIter
1132: 	if !newIterOpts.batch.batchOnly {
1133: 		// Grab and reference the current readState. This prevents the underlying
1134: 		// files in the associated version from being deleted if there is a current
1135: 		// compaction. The readState is unref'd by Iterator.Close().
1136: 		if newIterOpts.snapshot.vers == nil {
1137: 			if newIterOpts.snapshot.readState != nil {
1138: 				readState = newIterOpts.snapshot.readState
1139: 				readState.ref()
1140: 			} else {
1141: 				// NB: loadReadState() calls readState.ref().
1142: 				readState = d.loadReadState()
1143: 			}
1144: 		} else {
1145: 			// vers != nil
1146: 			newIterOpts.snapshot.vers.Ref()
1147: 		}
1148: 
1149: 		// Determine the seqnum to read at after grabbing the read state (current and
1150: 		// memtables) above.
1151: 		if seqNum == 0 {
1152: 			seqNum = d.mu.versions.visibleSeqNum.Load()
1153: 		}
1154: 		newIters = d.newIters
1155: 		newIterRangeKey = d.tableNewRangeKeyIter
1156: 	}
1157: 
1158: 	// Bundle various structures under a single umbrella in order to allocate
1159: 	// them together.
1160: 	var buf *iterAllocCommon
1161: 	if d.opts.IteratorStack == IteratorStackV2 {
1162: 		a := newIterV2Alloc()
1163: 		a.dbi.allocV2 = a
1164: 		buf = &a.iterAllocCommon
1165: 	} else {
1166: 		a := newIterAlloc()
1167: 		a.dbi.alloc = a
1168: 		buf = &a.iterAllocCommon
1169: 	}
1170: 	dbi := &buf.dbi
1171: 	dbi.closeChecker = invariants.CloseChecker{}
1172: 	dbi.ctx = ctx
1173: 	dbi.merge = d.merge
1174: 	dbi.comparer = d.opts.Comparer
1175: 	dbi.readState = readState
1176: 	dbi.version = newIterOpts.snapshot.vers
1177: 	dbi.keyBuf = buf.keyBuf
1178: 	dbi.prefixOrFullSeekKey = buf.prefixOrFullSeekKey
1179: 	dbi.boundsBuf = buf.boundsBuf
1180: 	dbi.fc = d.fileCache
1181: 	dbi.newIters = newIters
1182: 	dbi.newIterRangeKey = newIterRangeKey
1183: 	dbi.valueRetrievalProfile = d.valueRetrievalProfile.Load()
1184: 	dbi.seqNum = seqNum
1185: 	dbi.batchOnlyIter = newIterOpts.batch.batchOnly
1186: 	if o != nil {
1187: 		dbi.opts = *o
1188: 		dbi.processBounds(o.LowerBound, o.UpperBound)
1189: 	}
1190: 	dbi.opts.logger = d.opts.Logger
1191: 	if d.opts.private.disableLazyCombinedIteration {
1192: 		dbi.opts.disableLazyCombinedIteration = true
1193: 	}
1194: 	if batch != nil {
1195: 		dbi.batch = &buf.batchState
1196: 		dbi.batch.batch = batch
1197: 		dbi.batch.batchSeqNum = batch.nextSeqNum()
1198: 	}
1199: 	dbi.tracker = d.iterTracker
1200: 	if !dbi.batchOnlyIter && d.iterTracker != nil && !dbi.opts.ExemptFromTracking {
1201: 		dbi.trackerHandle = d.iterTracker.Start()
1202: 	}
1203: 	dbi.finishInitializingIter(ctx)
1204: 	return dbi
1205: }

1207: // finishInitializingIter does the non-trivial initialization of an Iterator.
1208: // It's invoked to perform the initial initialization of an Iterator during
1209: // NewIter or Clone, and to perform reinitialization due to a change in
1210: // IterOptions by a call to Iterator.SetOptions.
1211: func (dbi *Iterator) finishInitializingIter(ctx context.Context) {
1212: 	var memtables flushableList
1213: 	if dbi.readState != nil {
1214: 		memtables = dbi.readState.memtables
1215: 	}
1216: 	if dbi.opts.OnlyReadGuaranteedDurable {
1217: 		memtables = nil
1218: 	} else {
1219: 		// We only need to read from memtables which contain sequence numbers older
1220: 		// than seqNum. Trim off newer memtables.
1221: 		for i := len(memtables) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
1222: 			if logSeqNum := memtables[i].logSeqNum; logSeqNum < dbi.seqNum {
1223: 				break
1224: 			}
1225: 			memtables = memtables[:i]
1226: 		}
1227: 	}
1228: 
1229: 	if dbi.opts.pointKeys() {
1230: 		// Construct the point iterator, initializing dbi.pointIter to point to
1231: 		// dbi.merging. If this is called during a SetOptions call and this
1232: 		// Iterator has already initialized dbi.merging, constructPointIter is a
1233: 		// noop and an initialized pointIter already exists in dbi.pointIter.
1234: 		if dbi.pointIter == nil {
1235: 			internalOpts := dbi.makeInternalIterOpts(memtables)
1236: 			if dbi.allocV2 != nil {
1237: 				dbi.constructPointIterV2(ctx, memtables, internalOpts)
1238: 			} else {
1239: 				dbi.constructPointIter(ctx, memtables, internalOpts)
1240: 			}
1241: 		}
1242: 		dbi.iter = dbi.pointIter
1243: 	} else {
1244: 		dbi.iter = emptyIter
1245: 	}
1246: 
1247: 	if dbi.opts.rangeKeys() {
1248: 		dbi.rangeKeyMasking.init(dbi, dbi.comparer)
1249: 
1250: 		// When iterating over both point and range keys, don't create the
1251: 		// range-key iterator stack immediately if we can avoid it. This
1252: 		// optimization takes advantage of the expected sparseness of range
1253: 		// keys, and configures the point-key iterator to dynamically switch to
1254: 		// combined iteration when it observes a file containing range keys.
1255: 		//
1256: 		// Lazy combined iteration is not possible if a batch or a memtable
1257: 		// contains any range keys.
1258: 		useLazyCombinedIteration := dbi.rangeKey == nil &&
1259: 			dbi.opts.KeyTypes == IterKeyTypePointsAndRanges &&
1260: 			(dbi.batch == nil || dbi.batch.batch.countRangeKeys == 0) &&
1261: 			!dbi.batchOnlyIter &&
1262: 			!dbi.opts.disableLazyCombinedIteration
1263: 		if useLazyCombinedIteration {
1264: 			// The user requested combined iteration, and there's no indexed
1265: 			// batch currently containing range keys that would prevent lazy
1266: 			// combined iteration. Check the memtables to see if they contain

1756: // memtables referenced by the iterator from being deleted. Using an iterator
1757: // to maintain a long-lived point-in-time view of the DB state can lead to an
1758: // apparent memory and disk usage leak. Use snapshots (see NewSnapshot) for
1759: // point-in-time snapshots which avoids these problems.
1760: func (d *DB) NewIter(o *IterOptions) (*Iterator, error) {
1761: 	return d.NewIterWithContext(context.Background(), o)
1762: }
1763: 
1764: // NewIterWithContext is like NewIter, and additionally accepts a context for
1765: // tracing.
1766: func (d *DB) NewIterWithContext(ctx context.Context, o *IterOptions) (*Iterator, error) {
1767: 	return d.newIter(ctx, nil /* batch */, newIterOpts{}, o), nil
1768: }

1770: // NewSnapshot returns a point-in-time view of the current DB state. Iterators
1771: // created with this handle will all observe a stable snapshot of the current
1772: // DB state. The caller must call Snapshot.Close() when the snapshot is no
1773: // longer needed. Snapshots are not persisted across DB restarts (close ->
1774: // open). Unlike the implicit snapshot maintained by an iterator, a snapshot
1775: // will not prevent memtables from being released or sstables from being
1776: // deleted. Instead, a snapshot prevents deletion of sequence numbers
1777: // referenced by the snapshot.
1778: //
1779: // There exists one violation of a Snapshot's point-in-time guarantee: An excise
1780: // (see DB.Excise and DB.IngestAndExcise) that occurs after the snapshot's
1781: // creation will be observed by iterators created from the snapshot after the
1782: // excise. See NewEventuallyFileOnlySnapshot for a variant of NewSnapshot that
1783: // provides a full point-in-time guarantee.
1784: func (d *DB) NewSnapshot() *Snapshot {
1785: 	// TODO(jackson): Consider removal of regular, non-eventually-file-only
1786: 	// snapshots given they no longer provide a true point-in-time snapshot of
1787: 	// the database due to excises. If we had a mechanism to construct a maximal
1788: 	// key range, we could implement NewSnapshot in terms of
1789: 	// NewEventuallyFileOnlySnapshot and provide a true point-in-time guarantee.
1790: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1791: 		panic(err)
1792: 	}
1793: 	d.mu.Lock()
1794: 	s := &Snapshot{
1795: 		db:     d,
1796: 		seqNum: d.mu.versions.visibleSeqNum.Load(),
1797: 	}
1798: 	d.mu.snapshots.pushBack(s)
1799: 	d.mu.Unlock()
1800: 	return s
1801: }

1803: // NewEventuallyFileOnlySnapshot returns a point-in-time view of the current DB
1804: // state, similar to NewSnapshot, but with consistency constrained to the
1805: // provided set of key ranges. See the comment at EventuallyFileOnlySnapshot for
1806: // its semantics.
1807: func (d *DB) NewEventuallyFileOnlySnapshot(keyRanges []KeyRange) *EventuallyFileOnlySnapshot {
1808: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1809: 		panic(err)
1810: 	}
1811: 	for i := range keyRanges {
1812: 		if i > 0 && d.cmp(keyRanges[i-1].End, keyRanges[i].Start) > 0 {
1813: 			panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: key ranges for eventually-file-only-snapshot not in order"))
1814: 		}
1815: 	}
1816: 	return d.makeEventuallyFileOnlySnapshot(keyRanges)
1817: }

1819: // Close closes the DB.
1820: //
1821: // It is not safe to close a DB until all outstanding iterators are closed
1822: // or to call Close concurrently with any other DB method. It is not valid
1823: // to call any of a DB's methods after the DB has been closed.
1824: func (d *DB) Close() error {
1825: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1826: 		panic(err)
1827: 	}
1828: 	d.compactionSchedulers.Wait()
1829: 	// Compactions can be asynchronously started by the CompactionScheduler
1830: 	// calling d.Schedule. When this Unregister returns, we know that the
1831: 	// CompactionScheduler will never again call a method on the DB. Note that
1832: 	// this must be called without holding d.mu.
1833: 	d.compactionScheduler.Unregister()
1834: 	// Lock the commit pipeline for the duration of Close. This prevents a race
1835: 	// with makeRoomForWrite. Rotating the WAL in makeRoomForWrite requires
1836: 	// dropping d.mu several times for I/O. If Close only holds d.mu, an
1837: 	// in-progress WAL rotation may re-acquire d.mu only once the database is
1838: 	// closed.
1839: 	//
1840: 	// Additionally, locking the commit pipeline makes it more likely that
1841: 	// (illegal) concurrent writes will observe d.closed.Load() != nil, creating
1842: 	// more understable panics if the database is improperly used concurrently
1843: 	// during Close.
1844: 	d.commit.mu.Lock()
1845: 	defer d.commit.mu.Unlock()
1846: 	d.mu.Lock()
1847: 	defer d.mu.Unlock()
1848: 	// Check that the DB is not closed again. If there are two concurrent calls
1849: 	// to DB.Close, the best-effort check at the top of DB.Close may not fire.
1850: 	// But since this second check happens after mutex acquisition, the two
1851: 	// concurrent calls will get serialized and the second one will see the
1852: 	// effect of the d.closed.Store below.
1853: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1854: 		panic(err)
1855: 	}
1856: 	// Clear the finalizer that is used to check that an unreferenced DB has been
1857: 	// closed. We're closing the DB here, so the check performed by that
1858: 	// finalizer isn't necessary.
1859: 	//
1860: 	// Note: this is a no-op if invariants are disabled or race is enabled.
1861: 	invariants.SetFinalizer(d.closed, nil)
1862: 
1863: 	d.closed.Store(errors.WithStack(ErrClosed))
1864: 	close(d.closedCh)
1865: 	d.bgCtxCancel()
1866: 
1867: 	defer d.cacheHandle.Close()
1868: 
1869: 	for d.mu.compact.compactingCount > 0 || d.mu.compact.downloadingCount > 0 || d.mu.compact.flushing {
1870: 		d.mu.compact.cond.Wait()
1871: 	}
1872: 	for d.mu.tableStats.loading {
1873: 		d.mu.tableStats.cond.Wait()
1874: 	}
1875: 	for d.mu.tableValidation.validating {
1876: 		d.mu.tableValidation.cond.Wait()
1877: 	}
1878: 
1879: 	var err error
1880: 	if n := len(d.mu.compact.inProgress); n > 0 {
1881: 		err = errors.Errorf("pebble: %d unexpected in-progress compactions", errors.Safe(n))
1882: 	}
1883: 	err = firstError(err, d.mu.formatVers.marker.Close())
1884: 	if !d.opts.ReadOnly {
1885: 		if d.mu.log.writer != nil {
1886: 			_, err2 := d.mu.log.writer.Close()
1887: 			err = firstError(err, err2)
1888: 		}
1889: 	} else if d.mu.log.writer != nil {
1890: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: log-writer should be nil in read-only mode"))
1891: 	}
1892: 	err = firstError(err, d.mu.log.manager.Close())
1893: 
1894: 	// Note that versionSet.close() only closes the MANIFEST. The versions list
1895: 	// is still valid for the checks below.
1896: 	err = firstError(err, d.mu.versions.close())
1897: 
1898: 	d.readState.val.unrefLocked()
1899: 
1900: 	current := d.mu.versions.currentVersion()
1901: 	for v := d.mu.versions.versions.Front(); true; v = v.Next() {
1902: 		refs := v.Refs()
1903: 		if v == current {
1904: 			if refs != 1 {
1905: 				err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("leaked iterators: current\n%s", v))
1906: 			}
1907: 			break
1908: 		}
1909: 		if refs != 0 {
1910: 			err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("leaked iterators:\n%s", v))
1911: 		}
1912: 	}
1913: 
1914: 	for _, mem := range d.mu.mem.queue {
1915: 		// Usually, we'd want to delete the files returned by readerUnref. But
1916: 		// in this case, even if we're unreferencing the flushables, the
1917: 		// flushables aren't obsolete. They will be reconstructed during WAL
1918: 		// replay.
1919: 		mem.readerUnrefLocked(false)
1920: 	}
1921: 	// If there's an unused, recycled memtable, we need to release its memory.
1922: 	if obsoleteMemTable := d.memTableRecycle.Swap(nil); obsoleteMemTable != nil {
1923: 		d.freeMemTable(obsoleteMemTable)
1924: 	}
1925: 	if reserved := d.memTableReserved.Load(); reserved != 0 {
1926: 		err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("leaked memtable reservation: %d", errors.Safe(reserved)))
1927: 	}
1928: 
1929: 	// Since we called d.readState.val.unrefLocked() above, we are expected to
1930: 	// manually schedule deletion of obsolete files.
1931: 	if len(d.mu.versions.obsoleteTables) > 0 || len(d.mu.versions.obsoleteBlobs) > 0 {
1932: 		d.deleteObsoleteFiles(d.newJobIDLocked())
1933: 	}
1934: 
1935: 	d.mu.Unlock()
1936: 
1937: 	// Wait for all cleaning jobs to finish.
1938: 	d.deletePacer.Close()
1939: 
1940: 	d.mu.Lock()
1941: 	// Sanity check compaction metrics.
1942: 	if invariants.Enabled {
1943: 		if d.mu.compact.compactingCount > 0 || d.mu.compact.downloadingCount > 0 || d.mu.versions.atomicInProgressBytes.Load() > 0 {
1944: 			panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("compacting counts not 0 on close"))
1945: 		}
1946: 	}
1947: 
1948: 	// As a sanity check, ensure that there are no zombie tables or blob files.
1949: 	// A non-zero count hints at a reference count leak.
1950: 	if ztbls := d.mu.versions.zombieTables.Count(); ztbls > 0 {
1951: 		err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("non-zero zombie file count: %d", ztbls))
1952: 	}
1953: 	if zblobs := d.mu.versions.zombieBlobs.Count(); zblobs > 0 {
1954: 		err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("non-zero zombie blob count: %d", zblobs))
1955: 	}
1956: 
1957: 	err = firstError(err, d.fileCache.Close())
1958: 
1959: 	err = firstError(err, d.objProvider.Close())
1960: 
1961: 	// If the options include a closer to 'close' the filesystem, close it.
1962: 	if d.opts.private.fsCloser != nil {
1963: 		d.opts.private.fsCloser.Close()
1964: 	}
1965: 
1966: 	// Return an error if the user failed to close all open snapshots.
1967: 	if v := d.mu.snapshots.count(); v > 0 {
1968: 		err = firstError(err, errors.Errorf("leaked snapshots: %d open snapshots on DB %p", v, d))
1969: 	}
1970: 	err = firstError(err, d.dirs.Close())
1971: 
1972: 	if d.iterTracker != nil {
1973: 		d.iterTracker.Close()
1974: 		d.iterTracker = nil
1975: 	}
1976: 
1977: 	return err
1978: }

1980: // Compact the specified range of keys in the database.
1981: func (d *DB) Compact(ctx context.Context, start, end []byte, parallelize bool) error {
1982: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
1983: 		panic(err)
1984: 	}
1985: 	if d.opts.ReadOnly {
1986: 		return ErrReadOnly
1987: 	}
1988: 	if d.cmp(start, end) >= 0 {
1989: 		return errors.Errorf("Compact start %s is not less than end %s",
1990: 			d.opts.Comparer.FormatKey(start), d.opts.Comparer.FormatKey(end))
1991: 	}
1992: 
1993: 	d.mu.Lock()
1994: 	maxLevelWithFiles := 1
1995: 	cur := d.mu.versions.currentVersion()
1996: 	for level := 0; level < numLevels; level++ {
1997: 		overlaps := cur.Overlaps(level, base.UserKeyBoundsInclusive(start, end))
1998: 		if !overlaps.Empty() {
1999: 			maxLevelWithFiles = level + 1
2000: 		}
2001: 	}
2002: 
2003: 	// Determine if any memtable overlaps with the compaction range. We wait for
2004: 	// any such overlap to flush (initiating a flush if necessary).
2005: 	mem, err := func() (*flushableEntry, error) {
2006: 		// Check to see if any files overlap with any of the memtables. The queue
2007: 		// is ordered from oldest to newest with the mutable memtable being the
2008: 		// last element in the slice. We want to wait for the newest table that
2009: 		// overlaps.
2010: 		for i := len(d.mu.mem.queue) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
2011: 			mem := d.mu.mem.queue[i]
2012: 			var anyOverlaps bool
2013: 			mem.computePossibleOverlaps(func(b bounded) shouldContinue {
2014: 				anyOverlaps = true
2015: 				return stopIteration
2016: 			}, KeyRange{Start: start, End: end})
2017: 			if !anyOverlaps {
2018: 				continue
2019: 			}
2020: 			var err error
2021: 			if mem.flushable == d.mu.mem.mutable {
2022: 				// We have to hold both commitPipeline.mu and DB.mu when calling
2023: 				// makeRoomForWrite(). Lock order requirements elsewhere force us to
2024: 				// unlock DB.mu in order to grab commitPipeline.mu first.
2025: 				d.mu.Unlock()
2026: 				d.commit.mu.Lock()
2027: 				d.mu.Lock()
2028: 				defer d.commit.mu.Unlock() //nolint:deferloop
2029: 				if mem.flushable == d.mu.mem.mutable {
2030: 					// Only flush if the active memtable is unchanged.
2031: 					err = d.makeRoomForWrite(nil)
2032: 				}
2033: 			}
2034: 			mem.flushForced = true
2035: 			d.maybeScheduleFlush()
2036: 			return mem, err
2037: 		}
2038: 		return nil, nil
2039: 	}()
2040: 
2041: 	d.mu.Unlock()
2042: 
2043: 	if err != nil {
2044: 		return err
2045: 	}
2046: 	if mem != nil {
2047: 		select {
2048: 		case <-mem.flushed:
2049: 		case <-ctx.Done():
2050: 			return ctx.Err()
2051: 		}
2052: 	}
2053: 
2054: 	for level := 0; level < maxLevelWithFiles; {
2055: 		for {
2056: 			if err := d.manualCompact(
2057: 				ctx, start, end, level, parallelize); err != nil {
2058: 				if errors.Is(err, ErrCancelledCompaction) {
2059: 					continue
2060: 				}
2061: 				return err
2062: 			}
2063: 			break
2064: 		}
2065: 		level++
2066: 		if level == numLevels-1 {
2067: 			// A manual compaction of the bottommost level occurred.
2068: 			// There is no next level to try and compact.
2069: 			break
2070: 		}
2071: 	}
2072: 	return nil
2073: }

2075: func (d *DB) manualCompact(
2076: 	ctx context.Context, start, end []byte, level int, parallelize bool,
2077: ) error {
2078: 	d.mu.Lock()
2079: 	curr := d.mu.versions.currentVersion()
2080: 	files := curr.Overlaps(level, base.UserKeyBoundsInclusive(start, end))
2081: 	if files.Empty() {
2082: 		d.mu.Unlock()
2083: 		return nil
2084: 	}
2085: 
2086: 	var compactions []*manualCompaction
2087: 	if parallelize {
2088: 		compactions = append(compactions, d.splitManualCompaction(start, end, level)...)
2089: 	} else {
2090: 		compactions = append(compactions, &manualCompaction{
2091: 			level: level,
2092: 			done:  make(chan error, 1),
2093: 			start: start,
2094: 			end:   end,
2095: 		})
2096: 	}
2097: 	n := len(compactions)
2098: 	if n == 0 {
2099: 		d.mu.Unlock()
2100: 		return nil
2101: 	}
2102: 	for i := range compactions {
2103: 		d.mu.compact.manualID++
2104: 		compactions[i].id = d.mu.compact.manualID
2105: 	}
2106: 	// [manualIDStart, manualIDEnd] are the compactions that have been added to
2107: 	// d.mu.compact.manual.
2108: 	manualIDStart := compactions[0].id
2109: 	manualIDEnd := compactions[n-1].id
2110: 	d.mu.compact.manual = append(d.mu.compact.manual, compactions...)
2111: 	d.mu.compact.manualLen.Store(int32(len(d.mu.compact.manual)))
2112: 	d.maybeScheduleCompaction()
2113: 	d.mu.Unlock()
2114: 
2115: 	// On context cancellation, we only cancel the compactions that have not yet
2116: 	// started. The assumption is that it is relatively harmless to have the
2117: 	// already started compactions run to completion. We don't wait for the
2118: 	// ongoing compactions to finish, since the assumption is that the caller
2119: 	// has already given up on the operation (and the cancellation error is
2120: 	// going to be returned anyway).
2121: 	//
2122: 	// An alternative would be to store the context in each *manualCompaction,
2123: 	// and have the goroutine that retrieves the *manualCompaction for running
2124: 	// notice the cancellation and write the cancellation error to
2125: 	// manualCompaction.done. That approach would require this method to wait
2126: 	// for all the *manualCompactions it has enqueued to finish before returning
2127: 	// (to not leak a context). Since there is no timeliness guarantee on when a
2128: 	// *manualCompaction will be retrieved for running, the wait until a
2129: 	// cancelled context causes this method to return is not bounded. Hence, we
2130: 	// don't adopt that approach.
2131: 	cancelPendingCompactions := func() {
2132: 		d.mu.Lock()
2133: 		for i := 0; i < len(d.mu.compact.manual); {
2134: 			if d.mu.compact.manual[i].id >= manualIDStart && d.mu.compact.manual[i].id <= manualIDEnd {
2135: 				d.mu.compact.manual = slices.Delete(d.mu.compact.manual, i, i+1)
2136: 				d.mu.compact.manualLen.Store(int32(len(d.mu.compact.manual)))
2137: 			} else {
2138: 				i++
2139: 			}
2140: 		}
2141: 		d.mu.Unlock()
2142: 	}
2143: 	// Each of the channels is guaranteed to be eventually sent to once. After a
2144: 	// compaction is possibly picked in d.maybeScheduleCompaction(), either the
2145: 	// compaction is dropped, executed after being scheduled, or retried later.
2146: 	// Assuming eventual progress when a compaction is retried, all outcomes send
2147: 	// a value to the done channel. Since the channels are buffered, it is not
2148: 	// necessary to read from each channel, and so we can exit early in the event
2149: 	// of an error.
2150: 	for _, compaction := range compactions {
2151: 		select {
2152: 		case <-ctx.Done():
2153: 			cancelPendingCompactions()
2154: 			return ctx.Err()
2155: 		case err := <-compaction.done:
2156: 			if err != nil {
2157: 				cancelPendingCompactions()
2158: 				return err
2159: 			}
2160: 		}
2161: 	}
2162: 	return nil
2163: }

2165: // splitManualCompaction splits a manual compaction over [start,end] on level
2166: // such that the resulting compactions have no key overlap.
2167: func (d *DB) splitManualCompaction(
2168: 	start, end []byte, level int,
2169: ) (splitCompactions []*manualCompaction) {
2170: 	curr := d.mu.versions.currentVersion()
2171: 	endLevel := level + 1
2172: 	baseLevel := d.mu.versions.picker.getBaseLevel()
2173: 	if level == 0 {
2174: 		endLevel = baseLevel
2175: 	}
2176: 	keyRanges := curr.CalculateInuseKeyRanges(d.mu.versions.latest.l0Organizer, level, endLevel, start, end)
2177: 	for _, keyRange := range keyRanges {
2178: 		splitCompactions = append(splitCompactions, &manualCompaction{
2179: 			level: level,
2180: 			done:  make(chan error, 1),
2181: 			start: keyRange.Start,
2182: 			end:   keyRange.End.Key,
2183: 			split: true,
2184: 		})
2185: 	}
2186: 	return splitCompactions
2187: }

2189: // Flush the memtable to stable storage.
2190: func (d *DB) Flush() error {
2191: 	flushDone, err := d.AsyncFlush()
2192: 	if err != nil {
2193: 		return err
2194: 	}
2195: 	<-flushDone
2196: 	return nil
2197: }

2199: // AsyncFlush asynchronously flushes the memtable to stable storage.
2200: //
2201: // If no error is returned, the caller can receive from the returned channel in
2202: // order to wait for the flush to complete.
2203: func (d *DB) AsyncFlush() (<-chan struct{}, error) {
2204: 	if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
2205: 		panic(err)
2206: 	}
2207: 	if d.opts.ReadOnly {
2208: 		return nil, ErrReadOnly
2209: 	}
2210: 
2211: 	d.commit.mu.Lock()
2212: 	defer d.commit.mu.Unlock()
2213: 	d.mu.Lock()
2214: 	defer d.mu.Unlock()
2215: 	flushed := d.mu.mem.queue[len(d.mu.mem.queue)-1].flushed
2216: 	err := d.makeRoomForWrite(nil)
2217: 	if err != nil {
2218: 		return nil, err
2219: 	}
2220: 	return flushed, nil
2221: }

2252: 	for _, m := range d.mu.mem.queue {

2254: 	}
2255: 	metrics.Snapshots.Count = d.mu.snapshots.count()

2258: 	}
2259: 	metrics.Snapshots.PinnedKeys = d.mu.snapshots.cumulativePinnedCount
2260: 	metrics.Snapshots.PinnedSize = d.mu.snapshots.cumulativePinnedSize
2261: 	metrics.MemTable.Count = int64(len(d.mu.mem.queue))

2487: // SSTables retrieves the current sstables. The returned slice is indexed by
2488: // level and each level is indexed by the position of the sstable within the
2489: // level. Note that this information may be out of date due to concurrent
2490: // flushes and compactions.
2491: func (d *DB) SSTables(opts ...SSTablesOption) ([][]SSTableInfo, error) {
2492: 	opt := &sstablesOptions{}
2493: 	for _, fn := range opts {
2494: 		fn(opt)
2495: 	}
2496: 
2497: 	if opt.withApproximateSpanBytes && (opt.start == nil || opt.end == nil) {
2498: 		return nil, errors.Errorf("cannot use WithApproximateSpanBytes without WithKeyRangeFilter option")
2499: 	}
2500: 
2501: 	// Grab and reference the current readState.
2502: 	readState := d.loadReadState()
2503: 	defer readState.unref()
2504: 
2505: 	// TODO(peter): This is somewhat expensive, especially on a large
2506: 	// database. It might be worthwhile to unify TableInfo and TableMetadata and
2507: 	// then we could simply return current.Files. Note that RocksDB is doing
2508: 	// something similar to the current code, so perhaps it isn't too bad.
2509: 	srcLevels := readState.current.Levels
2510: 	var totalTables int
2511: 	for i := range srcLevels {
2512: 		totalTables += srcLevels[i].Len()
2513: 	}
2514: 
2515: 	destTables := make([]SSTableInfo, totalTables)
2516: 	destLevels := make([][]SSTableInfo, len(srcLevels))
2517: 	for i := range destLevels {
2518: 		j := 0
2519: 		for m := range srcLevels[i].All() {
2520: 			if opt.start != nil && opt.end != nil {
2521: 				b := base.UserKeyBoundsEndExclusive(opt.start, opt.end)
2522: 				if !m.Overlaps(d.opts.Comparer.Compare, &b) {
2523: 					continue
2524: 				}
2525: 			}
2526: 			destTables[j] = SSTableInfo{
2527: 				TableInfo: m.TableInfo(),
2528: 			}
2529: 			if stats, ok := m.Stats(); ok {
2530: 				destTables[j].TableStats = *stats
2531: 			}
2532: 			if opt.withProperties {
2533: 				p, err := d.fileCache.getTableProperties(
2534: 					m,
2535: 				)
2536: 				if err != nil {
2537: 					return nil, err
2538: 				}
2539: 				destTables[j].Properties = p
2540: 			}
2541: 			destTables[j].Virtual = m.Virtual
2542: 			destTables[j].BackingSSTNum = m.TableBacking.DiskFileNum
2543: 			destTables[j].BackingSize = m.TableBacking.Size
2544: 			objMeta, err := d.objProvider.Lookup(base.FileTypeTable, m.TableBacking.DiskFileNum)
2545: 			if err != nil {
2546: 				return nil, err
2547: 			}
2548: 			if objMeta.IsRemote() {
2549: 				if objMeta.IsShared() {
2550: 					if d.objProvider.IsSharedForeign(objMeta) {
2551: 						destTables[j].BackingType = BackingTypeSharedForeign
2552: 					} else {
2553: 						destTables[j].BackingType = BackingTypeShared
2554: 					}
2555: 				} else {
2556: 					destTables[j].BackingType = BackingTypeExternal
2557: 				}
2558: 				destTables[j].Locator = objMeta.Remote.Locator
2559: 			} else {
2560: 				destTables[j].BackingType = BackingTypeLocal
2561: 			}
2562: 
2563: 			if opt.withApproximateSpanBytes {
2564: 				if m.ContainedWithinSpan(d.opts.Comparer.Compare, opt.start, opt.end) {
2565: 					destTables[j].ApproximateSpanBytes = m.Size
2566: 				} else {
2567: 					size, err := d.fileCache.estimateSize(m, opt.start, opt.end)
2568: 					if err != nil {
2569: 						return nil, err
2570: 					}
2571: 					destTables[j].ApproximateSpanBytes = size
2572: 				}
2573: 			}
2574: 			j++
2575: 		}
2576: 		destLevels[i] = destTables[:j]
2577: 		destTables = destTables[j:]
2578: 	}
2579: 
2580: 	return destLevels, nil
2581: }

2597: func (d *DB) newMemTable(
2598: 	logNum base.DiskFileNum, logSeqNum base.SeqNum, minSize uint64,
2599: ) (*memTable, *flushableEntry) {
2600: 	targetSize := minSize + uint64(memTableEmptySize)
2601: 	// The targetSize should be less than MemTableSize, because any batch >=
2602: 	// MemTableSize/2 should be treated as a large flushable batch.
2603: 	if targetSize > d.opts.MemTableSize {
2604: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("attempting to allocate memtable larger than MemTableSize"))
2605: 	}
2606: 	// Double until the next memtable size is at least large enough to fit
2607: 	// minSize.
2608: 	for d.mu.mem.nextSize < targetSize {
2609: 		d.mu.mem.nextSize = min(2*d.mu.mem.nextSize, d.opts.MemTableSize)
2610: 	}
2611: 	size := d.mu.mem.nextSize
2612: 	// The next memtable should be double the size, up to Options.MemTableSize.
2613: 	if d.mu.mem.nextSize < d.opts.MemTableSize {
2614: 		d.mu.mem.nextSize = min(2*d.mu.mem.nextSize, d.opts.MemTableSize)
2615: 	}
2616: 
2617: 	memtblOpts := memTableOptions{
2618: 		Options:   d.opts,
2619: 		logSeqNum: logSeqNum,
2620: 	}
2621: 
2622: 	// Before attempting to allocate a new memtable, check if there's one
2623: 	// available for recycling in memTableRecycle. Large contiguous allocations
2624: 	// can be costly as fragmentation makes it more difficult to find a large
2625: 	// contiguous free space. We've observed 64MB allocations taking 10ms+.
2626: 	//
2627: 	// To reduce these costly allocations, up to 1 obsolete memtable is stashed
2628: 	// in `d.memTableRecycle` to allow a future memtable rotation to reuse
2629: 	// existing memory.
2630: 	var mem *memTable
2631: 	mem = d.memTableRecycle.Swap(nil)
2632: 	if mem != nil && uint64(mem.arenaBuf.Len()) != size {
2633: 		d.freeMemTable(mem)
2634: 		mem = nil
2635: 	}
2636: 	if mem != nil {
2637: 		// Carry through the existing buffer and memory reservation.
2638: 		memtblOpts.arenaBuf = mem.arenaBuf
2639: 		memtblOpts.releaseAccountingReservation = mem.releaseAccountingReservation
2640: 	} else {
2641: 		mem = new(memTable)
2642: 		memtblOpts.arenaBuf = manual.New(manual.MemTable, uintptr(size))
2643: 		memtblOpts.releaseAccountingReservation = d.opts.Cache.Reserve(int(size))
2644: 		d.memTableCount.Add(1)
2645: 		d.memTableReserved.Add(int64(size))
2646: 
2647: 		// Note: this is a no-op if invariants are disabled or race is enabled.
2648: 		invariants.SetFinalizer(mem, checkMemTable)
2649: 	}
2650: 	mem.init(memtblOpts)
2651: 
2652: 	entry := d.newFlushableEntry(mem, logNum, logSeqNum)
2653: 	entry.releaseMemAccounting = func() {
2654: 		// If the user leaks iterators, we may be releasing the memtable after
2655: 		// the DB is already closed. In this case, we want to just release the
2656: 		// memory because DB.Close won't come along to free it for us.
2657: 		if err := d.closed.Load(); err != nil {
2658: 			d.freeMemTable(mem)
2659: 			return
2660: 		}
2661: 
2662: 		// The next memtable allocation might be able to reuse this memtable.
2663: 		// Stash it on d.memTableRecycle.
2664: 		if unusedMem := d.memTableRecycle.Swap(mem); unusedMem != nil {
2665: 			// There was already a memtable waiting to be recycled. We're now
2666: 			// responsible for freeing it.
2667: 			d.freeMemTable(unusedMem)
2668: 		}
2669: 	}
2670: 	return mem, entry
2671: }

2673: func (d *DB) freeMemTable(m *memTable) {
2674: 	d.memTableCount.Add(-1)
2675: 	d.memTableReserved.Add(-int64(m.arenaBuf.Len()))
2676: 	m.free()
