2694: // maybeInduceWriteStall is called before performing a memtable rotation in
2695: // makeRoomForWrite. In some conditions, we prefer to stall the user's write
2696: // workload rather than continuing to accept writes that may result in resource
2697: // exhaustion or prohibitively slow reads.
2698: //
2699: // There are a couple reasons we might wait to rotate the memtable and
2700: // instead induce a write stall:
2701: //  1. If too many memtables have queued, we wait for a flush to finish before
2702: //     creating another memtable.
2703: //  2. If L0 read amplification has grown too high, we wait for compactions
2704: //     to reduce the read amplification before accepting more writes that will
2705: //     increase write pressure.
2706: //
2707: // maybeInduceWriteStall checks these stall conditions, and if present, waits
2708: // for them to abate.
2709: func (d *DB) maybeInduceWriteStall(b *Batch) {
2710: 	stalled := false
2711: 	// This function will call EventListener.WriteStallBegin at most once.  If
2712: 	// it does call it, it will call EventListener.WriteStallEnd once before
2713: 	// returning.
2714: 	var timer *time.Timer
2715: 	for {
2716: 		var size uint64
2717: 		for i := range d.mu.mem.queue {
2718: 			size += d.mu.mem.queue[i].totalBytes()
2719: 		}
2720: 		if size >= uint64(d.opts.MemTableStopWritesThreshold)*d.opts.MemTableSize &&
2721: 			!d.mu.log.manager.ElevateWriteStallThresholdForFailover() {
2722: 			// We have filled up the current memtable, but already queued memtables
2723: 			// are still flushing, so we wait.
2724: 			if !stalled {
2725: 				stalled = true
2726: 				d.opts.EventListener.WriteStallBegin(WriteStallBeginInfo{
2727: 					Reason: "memtable count limit reached",
2728: 				})
2729: 			}
2730: 			beforeWait := crtime.NowMono()
2731: 			// NB: In a rare case, we can start a write stall, and then the system
2732: 			// may detect WAL failover, resulting in
2733: 			// ElevateWriteStallThresholdForFailover returning true. So we want to
2734: 			// recheck the predicate periodically, which we do by signaling the
2735: 			// condition variable.
2736: 			if timer == nil {
2737: 				timer = time.AfterFunc(time.Second, d.mu.compact.cond.Broadcast)
2738: 			} else {
2739: 				timer.Reset(time.Second)
2740: 			}
2741: 			d.mu.compact.cond.Wait()
2742: 			timer.Stop()
2743: 			if b != nil {
2744: 				b.commitStats.MemTableWriteStallDuration += beforeWait.Elapsed()
2745: 			}
2746: 			continue
2747: 		}

19: // commitQueue is a lock-free fixed-size single-producer, multi-consumer
20: // queue. The single producer can enqueue (push) to the head, and consumers can
21: // dequeue (pop) from the tail.
22: //
23: // It has the added feature that it nils out unused slots to avoid unnecessary
24: // retention of objects.
25: type commitQueue struct {
26: 	// headTail packs together a 32-bit head index and a 32-bit tail index. Both
27: 	// are indexes into slots modulo len(slots)-1.
28: 	//
29: 	// tail = index of oldest data in queue
30: 	// head = index of next slot to fill
31: 	//
32: 	// Slots in the range [tail, head) are owned by consumers.  A consumer
33: 	// continues to own a slot outside this range until it nils the slot, at
34: 	// which point ownership passes to the producer.
35: 	//
36: 	// The head index is stored in the most-significant bits so that we can
37: 	// atomically add to it and the overflow is harmless.
38: 	headTail atomic.Uint64
39: 
40: 	// slots is a ring buffer of values stored in this queue. The size must be a
41: 	// power of 2. A slot is in use until *both* the tail index has moved beyond
42: 	// it and the slot value has been set to nil. The slot value is set to nil
43: 	// atomically by the consumer and read atomically by the producer.
44: 	slots [record.SyncConcurrency]atomic.Pointer[Batch]
45: }
46: 
47: const dequeueBits = 32
48: 
49: func (q *commitQueue) unpack(ptrs uint64) (head, tail uint32) {
50: 	const mask = 1<<dequeueBits - 1
51: 	head = uint32((ptrs >> dequeueBits) & mask)
52: 	tail = uint32(ptrs & mask)
53: 	return
54: }
55: 
56: func (q *commitQueue) pack(head, tail uint32) uint64 {
57: 	const mask = 1<<dequeueBits - 1
58: 	return (uint64(head) << dequeueBits) |
59: 		uint64(tail&mask)
60: }
61: 
62: func (q *commitQueue) enqueue(b *Batch) {
63: 	ptrs := q.headTail.Load()
64: 	head, tail := q.unpack(ptrs)
65: 	if (tail+uint32(len(q.slots)))&(1<<dequeueBits-1) == head {
66: 		// Queue is full. This should never be reached because commitPipeline.commitQueueSem
67: 		// limits the number of concurrent operations.
68: 		panic(errors.AssertionFailedf("pebble: not reached"))
69: 	}
70: 	slot := &q.slots[head&uint32(len(q.slots)-1)]
71: 
72: 	// Check if the head slot has been released by dequeueApplied.
73: 	for slot.Load() != nil {
74: 		// Another goroutine is still cleaning up the tail, so the queue is
75: 		// actually still full. We spin because this should resolve itself
76: 		// momentarily.
77: 		runtime.Gosched()
78: 	}
79: 
80: 	// The head slot is free, so we own it.
81: 	slot.Store(b)
82: 
83: 	// Increment head. This passes ownership of slot to dequeueApplied and acts as a
84: 	// store barrier for writing the slot.
85: 	q.headTail.Add(1 << dequeueBits)
86: }
87: 
88: // dequeueApplied removes the earliest enqueued Batch, if it is applied.
89: //
90: // Returns nil if the commit queue is empty or the earliest Batch is not yet
91: // applied.
92: func (q *commitQueue) dequeueApplied() *Batch {
93: 	for {
94: 		ptrs := q.headTail.Load()
95: 		head, tail := q.unpack(ptrs)
96: 		if tail == head {
97: 			// Queue is empty.
98: 			return nil
99: 		}
100: 
101: 		slot := &q.slots[tail&uint32(len(q.slots)-1)]
102: 		b := slot.Load()
103: 		if b == nil || !b.applied.Load() {
104: 			// The batch is not ready to be dequeued, or another goroutine has
105: 			// already dequeued it.
106: 			return nil
107: 		}
108: 
109: 		// Confirm head and tail (for our speculative check above) and increment
110: 		// tail. If this succeeds, then we own the slot at tail.
111: 		ptrs2 := q.pack(head, tail+1)
112: 		if q.headTail.CompareAndSwap(ptrs, ptrs2) {
113: 			// We now own slot.
114: 			//
115: 			// Tell enqueue that we're done with this slot. Zeroing the slot is also
116: 			// important so we don't leave behind references that could keep this object
117: 			// live longer than necessary.
118: 			slot.Store(nil)
119: 			// At this point enqueue owns the slot.
120: 			return b
121: 		}
122: 	}
123: }

126: // with. This allows fine-grained testing of commitPipeline behavior without

130: 	// commitPipeline.mu.
131: 	logSeqNum *base.AtomicSeqNum

133: 	// upwards atomically as batches are applied to the memtable.
134: 	visibleSeqNum *base.AtomicSeqNum
135:

137: 	apply func(b *Batch, mem *memTable) error

139: 	// asynchronously and done will be called on wg upon completion. If wg != nil
140: 	// and err != nil, a failure to persist the WAL will populate *err. Returns
141: 	// the memtable the batch should be applied to. Serial execution enforced by
142: 	// commitPipeline.mu.
143: 	write func(b *Batch, wg *sync.WaitGroup, err *error) (*memTable, error)
144: }

146: // A commitPipeline manages the stages of committing a set of mutations
147: // (contained in a single Batch) atomically to the DB. The steps are
148: // conceptually:
149: //
150: //  1. Write the batch to the WAL and optionally sync the WAL
151: //  2. Apply the mutations in the batch to the memtable
152: //
153: // These two simple steps are made complicated by the desire for high
154: // performance. In the absence of concurrency, performance is limited by how
155: // fast a batch can be written (and synced) to the WAL and then added to the
156: // memtable, both of which are outside the purview of the commit
157: // pipeline. Performance under concurrency is the primary concern of the commit
158: // pipeline, though it also needs to maintain two invariants:
159: //
160: //  1. Batches need to be written to the WAL in sequence number order.
161: //  2. Batches need to be made visible for reads in sequence number order. This
162: //     invariant arises from the use of a single sequence number which
163: //     indicates which mutations are visible.
164: //
165: // Taking these invariants into account, let's revisit the work the commit
166: // pipeline needs to perform. Writing the batch to the WAL is necessarily
167: // serialized as there is a single WAL object. The order of the entries in the
168: // WAL defines the sequence number order. Note that writing to the WAL is
169: // extremely fast, usually just a memory copy. Applying the mutations in a
170: // batch to the memtable can occur concurrently as the underlying skiplist
171: // supports concurrent insertions. Publishing the visible sequence number is
172: // another serialization point, but one with a twist: the visible sequence
173: // number cannot be bumped until the mutations for earlier batches have
174: // finished applying to the memtable (the visible sequence number only ratchets
175: // up). Lastly, if requested, the commit waits for the WAL to sync. Note that
176: // waiting for the WAL sync after ratcheting the visible sequence number allows
177: // another goroutine to read committed data before the WAL has synced. This is
178: // similar behavior to RocksDB's manual WAL flush functionality. Application
179: // code needs to protect against this if necessary.
180: //
181: // The full outline of the commit pipeline operation is as follows:
182: //
183: //	with commitPipeline mutex locked:
184: //	  assign batch sequence number
185: //	  write batch to WAL
186: //	(optionally) add batch to WAL sync list
187: //	apply batch to memtable (concurrently)
188: //	wait for earlier batches to apply
189: //	ratchet read sequence number
190: //	(optionally) wait for the WAL to sync
191: //
192: // As soon as a batch has been written to the WAL, the commitPipeline mutex is
193: // released allowing another batch to write to the WAL. Each commit operation
194: // individually applies its batch to the memtable providing concurrency. The
195: // WAL sync happens concurrently with applying to the memtable (see
196: // commitPipeline.syncLoop).
197: //
198: // The "waits for earlier batches to apply" work is more complicated than might
199: // be expected. The obvious approach would be to keep a queue of pending
200: // batches and for each batch to wait for the previous batch to finish
201: // committing. This approach was tried initially and turned out to be too
202: // slow. The problem is that it causes excessive goroutine activity as each
203: // committing goroutine needs to wake up in order for the next goroutine to be
204: // unblocked. The approach taken in the current code is conceptually similar,
205: // though it avoids waking a goroutine to perform work that another goroutine
206: // can perform. A commitQueue (a single-producer, multiple-consumer queue)
207: // holds the ordered list of committing batches. Addition to the queue is done
208: // while holding commitPipeline.mutex ensuring the same ordering of batches in
209: // the queue as the ordering in the WAL. When a batch finishes applying to the
210: // memtable, it atomically updates its Batch.applied field. Ratcheting of the
211: // visible sequence number is done by commitPipeline.publish which loops
212: // dequeueing "applied" batches and ratcheting the visible sequence number. If
213: // we hit an unapplied batch at the head of the queue we can block as we know
214: // that committing of that unapplied batch will eventually find our (applied)
215: // batch in the queue. See commitPipeline.publish for additional commentary.
216: type commitPipeline struct {
217: 	// WARNING: The following struct `commitQueue` contains fields which will
218: 	// be accessed atomically.
219: 	//
220: 	// Go allocations are guaranteed to be 64-bit aligned which we take advantage
221: 	// of by placing the 64-bit fields which we access atomically at the beginning
222: 	// of the commitPipeline struct.
223: 	// For more information, see https://golang.org/pkg/sync/atomic/#pkg-note-BUG.
224: 	// Queue of pending batches to commit.
225: 	pending commitQueue
226: 	env     commitEnv
227: 	// The commit path has two queues:
228: 	// - commitPipeline.pending contains batches whose seqnums have not yet been
229: 	//   published. It is a lock-free single producer multi consumer queue.
230: 	// - LogWriter.flusher.syncQ contains state for batches that have asked for
231: 	//   a sync. It is a lock-free single producer single consumer queue.
232: 	// These lock-free queues have a fixed capacity. And since they are
233: 	// lock-free, we cannot do blocking waits when pushing onto these queues, in
234: 	// case they are full. Additionally, adding to these queues happens while
235: 	// holding commitPipeline.mu, and we don't want to block while holding that
236: 	// mutex since it is also needed by other code.
237: 	//
238: 	// Popping from these queues is independent and for a particular batch can
239: 	// occur in either order, though it is more common that popping from the
240: 	// commitPipeline.pending will happen first.
241: 	//
242: 	// Due to these constraints, we reserve a unit of space in each queue before
243: 	// acquiring commitPipeline.mu, which also ensures that the push operation
244: 	// is guaranteed to have space in the queue. The commitQueueSem and
245: 	// logSyncQSem are used for this reservation.
246: 	commitQueueSem chan struct{}
247: 	logSyncQSem    chan struct{}
248: 	ingestSem      chan struct{}
249: 	// The mutex to use for synchronizing access to logSeqNum and serializing
250: 	// calls to commitEnv.write().
251: 	mu sync.Mutex
252: }
253: 
254: func newCommitPipeline(env commitEnv) *commitPipeline {
255: 	p := &commitPipeline{
256: 		env: env,
257: 		// The capacity of both commitQueue.slots and syncQueue.slots is set to
258: 		// record.SyncConcurrency, which also determines the value of these
259: 		// semaphores. We used to have a single semaphore, which required that the
260: 		// capacity of these queues be the same. Now that we have two semaphores,
261: 		// the capacity of these queues could be changed to be different. Say half
262: 		// of the batches asked to be synced, but syncing took 5x the latency of
263: 		// adding to the memtable and publishing. Then syncQueue.slots could be
264: 		// sized as 0.5*5 of the commitQueue.slots. We can explore this if we find
265: 		// that LogWriterMetrics.SyncQueueLen has high utilization under some
266: 		// workloads.
267: 		//
268: 		// NB: the commit concurrency is one less than SyncConcurrency because we
269: 		// have to allow one "slot" for a concurrent WAL rotation which will close
270: 		// and sync the WAL.
271: 		commitQueueSem: make(chan struct{}, record.SyncConcurrency-1),
272: 		logSyncQSem:    make(chan struct{}, record.SyncConcurrency-1),
273: 		ingestSem:      make(chan struct{}, 1),
274: 	}
275: 	return p
276: }
277: 
278: // directWrite is used to directly write to the WAL. commitPipeline.mu must be
279: // held while this is called. DB.mu must not be held. directWrite will only
280: // return once the WAL sync is complete. Note that DirectWrite is a special case
281: // function which is currently only used when ingesting sstables as a flushable.
282: // Reason carefully about the correctness argument when calling this function
283: // from any context.
284: func (p *commitPipeline) directWrite(b *Batch) error {
285: 	var syncWG sync.WaitGroup
286: 	var syncErr error
287: 	syncWG.Add(1)
288: 	p.logSyncQSem <- struct{}{}
289: 	_, err := p.env.write(b, &syncWG, &syncErr)
290: 	syncWG.Wait()
291: 	err = firstError(err, syncErr)
292: 	return err
293: }
294: 
295: // Commit the specified batch, writing it to the WAL, optionally syncing the
296: // WAL, and applying the batch to the memtable. Upon successful return the
297: // batch's mutations will be visible for reading.
298: // REQUIRES: noSyncWait => syncWAL
299: func (p *commitPipeline) Commit(b *Batch, syncWAL bool, noSyncWait bool) error {
300: 	if b.Empty() {
301: 		return nil
302: 	}
303: 
304: 	commitStartTime := crtime.NowMono()
305: 	// Acquire semaphores.
306: 	p.commitQueueSem <- struct{}{}
307: 	if syncWAL {
308: 		p.logSyncQSem <- struct{}{}
309: 	}
310: 	b.commitStats.SemaphoreWaitDuration = commitStartTime.Elapsed()
311: 
312: 	// Prepare the batch for committing: enqueuing the batch in the pending
313: 	// queue, determining the batch sequence number and writing the data to the
314: 	// WAL.
315: 	//
316: 	// NB: We set Batch.commitErr on error so that the batch won't be a candidate
317: 	// for reuse. See Batch.release().
318: 	mem, err := p.prepare(b, syncWAL, noSyncWait)
319: 	if err != nil {
320: 		b.db = nil // prevent batch reuse on error
321: 		// NB: we are not doing <-p.commitQueueSem since the batch is still
322: 		// sitting in the pending queue. We should consider fixing this by also
323: 		// removing the batch from the pending queue.
324: 		return err
325: 	}
326: 
327: 	// Apply the batch to the memtable.
328: 	if err := p.env.apply(b, mem); err != nil {
329: 		b.db = nil // prevent batch reuse on error
330: 		// NB: we are not doing <-p.commitQueueSem since the batch is still
331: 		// sitting in the pending queue. We should consider fixing this by also
332: 		// removing the batch from the pending queue.
333: 		return err
334: 	}
335: 
336: 	// Publish the batch sequence number.
337: 	p.publish(b)
338: 
339: 	<-p.commitQueueSem
340: 
341: 	if !noSyncWait {
342: 		// Already waited for commit, so look at the error.
343: 		if b.commitErr != nil {
344: 			b.db = nil // prevent batch reuse on error
345: 			err = b.commitErr
346: 		}
347: 	}
348: 	// Else noSyncWait. The LogWriter can be concurrently writing to
349: 	// b.commitErr. We will read b.commitErr in Batch.SyncWait after the
350: 	// LogWriter is done writing.
351: 
352: 	b.commitStats.TotalDuration = commitStartTime.Elapsed()
353: 
354: 	return err
355: }

357: // AllocateSeqNum allocates count sequence numbers, invokes the prepare
358: // callback, then the apply callback, and then publishes the sequence
359: // numbers. AllocateSeqNum does not write to the WAL or add entries to the
360: // memtable. AllocateSeqNum can be used to sequence an operation such as
361: // sstable ingestion within the commit pipeline. The prepare callback is
362: // invoked with commitPipeline.mu held, but note that DB.mu is not held and
363: // must be locked if necessary.
364: func (p *commitPipeline) AllocateSeqNum(
365: 	count int, prepare func(seqNum base.SeqNum), apply func(seqNum base.SeqNum),
366: ) {
367: 	// This method is similar to Commit and prepare. Be careful about trying to
368: 	// share additional code with those methods because Commit and prepare are
369: 	// performance critical code paths.
370: 
371: 	b := newBatch(nil)
372: 	defer func() { _ = b.Close() }()
373: 
374: 	// Give the batch a count of 1 so that the log and visible sequence number
375: 	// are incremented correctly.
376: 	b.data = make([]byte, batchrepr.HeaderLen)
377: 	b.setCount(uint32(count))
378: 	b.commit.Add(1)
379: 
380: 	p.commitQueueSem <- struct{}{}
381: 
382: 	p.mu.Lock()
383: 
384: 	// Enqueue the batch in the pending queue. Note that while the pending queue
385: 	// is lock-free, we want the order of batches to be the same as the sequence
386: 	// number order.
387: 	p.pending.enqueue(b)
388: 
389: 	// Assign the batch a sequence number. Note that we use atomic operations
390: 	// here to handle concurrent reads of logSeqNum. commitPipeline.mu provides
391: 	// mutual exclusion for other goroutines writing to logSeqNum.
392: 	logSeqNum := p.env.logSeqNum.Add(base.SeqNum(count)) - base.SeqNum(count)
393: 	seqNum := logSeqNum
394: 	if seqNum == 0 {
395: 		// We can't use the value 0 for the global seqnum during ingestion, because
396: 		// 0 indicates no global seqnum. So allocate one more seqnum.
397: 		p.env.logSeqNum.Add(1)
398: 		seqNum++
399: 	}
400: 	b.setSeqNum(seqNum)
401: 
402: 	// Wait for any outstanding writes to the memtable to complete. This is
403: 	// necessary for ingestion so that the check for memtable overlap can see any
404: 	// writes that were sequenced before the ingestion. The spin loop is
405: 	// unfortunate, but obviates the need for additional synchronization.
406: 	for {
407: 		visibleSeqNum := p.env.visibleSeqNum.Load()
408: 		if visibleSeqNum == logSeqNum {
409: 			break
410: 		}
411: 		runtime.Gosched()
412: 	}
413: 
414: 	// Invoke the prepare callback. Note the lack of error reporting. Even if the
415: 	// callback internally fails, the sequence number needs to be published in
416: 	// order to allow the commit pipeline to proceed.
417: 	prepare(b.SeqNum())
418: 
419: 	p.mu.Unlock()
420: 
421: 	// Invoke the apply callback.
422: 	apply(b.SeqNum())
423: 
424: 	// Publish the sequence number.
425: 	p.publish(b)
426: 
427: 	<-p.commitQueueSem
428: }

430: func (p *commitPipeline) prepare(b *Batch, syncWAL bool, noSyncWait bool) (*memTable, error) {
431: 	n := uint64(b.Count())
432: 	if n == invalidBatchCount {
433: 		return nil, ErrInvalidBatch
434: 	}
435: 	var syncWG *sync.WaitGroup
436: 	var syncErr *error
437: 	switch {
438: 	case !syncWAL:
439: 		// Only need to wait for the publish.
440: 		b.commit.Add(1)
441: 	// Remaining cases represent syncWAL=true.
442: 	case noSyncWait:
443: 		syncErr = &b.commitErr
444: 		syncWG = &b.fsyncWait
445: 		// Only need to wait synchronously for the publish. The user will
446: 		// (asynchronously) wait on the batch's fsyncWait.
447: 		b.commit.Add(1)
448: 		b.fsyncWait.Add(1)
449: 	case !noSyncWait:
450: 		syncErr = &b.commitErr
451: 		syncWG = &b.commit
452: 		// Must wait for both the publish and the WAL fsync.
453: 		b.commit.Add(2)
454: 	}
455: 
456: 	p.mu.Lock()
457: 
458: 	// Enqueue the batch in the pending queue. Note that while the pending queue
459: 	// is lock-free, we want the order of batches to be the same as the sequence
460: 	// number order.
461: 	p.pending.enqueue(b)
462: 
463: 	// Assign the batch a sequence number. Note that we use atomic operations
464: 	// here to handle concurrent reads of logSeqNum. commitPipeline.mu provides
465: 	// mutual exclusion for other goroutines writing to logSeqNum.
466: 	b.setSeqNum(p.env.logSeqNum.Add(base.SeqNum(n)) - base.SeqNum(n))
467: 
468: 	// Write the data to the WAL.
469: 	mem, err := p.env.write(b, syncWG, syncErr)
470: 
471: 	p.mu.Unlock()
472: 
473: 	return mem, err
474: }

476: func (p *commitPipeline) publish(b *Batch) {
477: 	// Mark the batch as applied.
478: 	b.applied.Store(true)
479: 
480: 	// Loop dequeuing applied batches from the pending queue. If our batch was
481: 	// the head of the pending queue we are guaranteed that either we'll publish
482: 	// it or someone else will dequeueApplied and publish it. If our batch is not the
483: 	// head of the queue then either we'll dequeueApplied applied batches and reach our
484: 	// batch or there is an unapplied batch blocking us. When that unapplied
485: 	// batch applies it will go through the same process and publish our batch
486: 	// for us.
487: 	for {
488: 		t := p.pending.dequeueApplied()
489: 		if t == nil {
490: 			// Wait for another goroutine to publish us. We might also be waiting for
491: 			// the WAL sync to finish.
492: 			now := crtime.NowMono()
493: 			b.commit.Wait()
494: 			b.commitStats.CommitWaitDuration += now.Elapsed()
495: 			break
496: 		}
497: 		if !t.applied.Load() {

501: 		// We're responsible for publishing the sequence number for batch t, but
502: 		// another concurrent goroutine might sneak in and publish the sequence
503: 		// number for a subsequent batch. That's ok as all we're guaranteeing is
504: 		// that the sequence number ratchets up.
505: 		for {
506: 			curSeqNum := p.env.visibleSeqNum.Load()
507: 			newSeqNum := t.SeqNum() + base.SeqNum(t.Count())
508: 			if newSeqNum <= curSeqNum {
509: 				// t's sequence number has already been published.
510: 				break
511: 			}
512: 			if p.env.visibleSeqNum.CompareAndSwap(curSeqNum, newSeqNum) {
513: 				// We successfully published t's sequence number.
514: 				break
515: 			}
516: 		}

518: 		t.commit.Done()

33: // iterPos describes the state of the internal iterator, in terms of whether it
34: // is at the position returned to the user (cur), one ahead of the position
35: // returned (next for forward iteration and prev for reverse iteration). The cur
36: // position is split into two states, for forward and reverse iteration, since
37: // we need to differentiate for switching directions.
38: //
39: // There is subtlety in what is considered the current position of the Iterator.
40: // The internal iterator exposes a sequence of internal keys. There is not
41: // always a single internalIterator position corresponding to the position
42: // returned to the user. Consider the example:
43: //
44: //	a.MERGE.9 a.MERGE.8 a.MERGE.7 a.SET.6 b.DELETE.9 b.DELETE.5 b.SET.4
45: //	\                                   /
46: //	  \       Iterator.Key() = 'a'    /
47: //
48: // The Iterator exposes one valid position at user key 'a' and the two exhausted
49: // positions at the beginning and end of iteration. The underlying
50: // internalIterator contains 7 valid positions and 2 exhausted positions.
51: //
52: // Iterator positioning methods must set iterPos to iterPosCur{Foward,Backward}
53: // iff the user key at the current internalIterator position equals the
54: // Iterator.Key returned to the user. This guarantees that a call to nextUserKey
55: // or prevUserKey will advance to the next or previous iterator position.
56: // iterPosCur{Forward,Backward} does not make any guarantee about the internal
57: // iterator position among internal keys with matching user keys, and it will
58: // vary subtly depending on the particular key kinds encountered. In the above
59: // example, the iterator returning 'a' may set iterPosCurForward if the internal
60: // iterator is positioned at any of a.MERGE.9, a.MERGE.8, a.MERGE.7 or a.SET.6.
61: //
62: // When setting iterPos to iterPosNext or iterPosPrev, the internal iterator
63: // must be advanced to the first internalIterator position at a user key greater
64: // (iterPosNext) or less (iterPosPrev) than the key returned to the user. An
65: // internalIterator position that's !Valid() must also be considered greater or
66: // less—depending on the direction of iteration—than the last valid Iterator
67: // position.

526: // Limited iteration mode. Not for use with prefix iteration.
527: //
528: // SeekGE, SeekLT, Prev, Next have WithLimit variants, that pause the iterator
529: // at the limit in a best-effort manner. The client should behave correctly
530: // even if the limits are ignored. These limits are not "deep", in that they
531: // are not passed down to the underlying collection of internalIterators. This
532: // is because the limits are transient, and apply only until the next
533: // iteration call. They serve mainly as a way to bound the amount of work when
534: // two (or more) Iterators are being coordinated at a higher level.
535: //
536: // In limited iteration mode:
537: // - Avoid using Iterator.Valid if the last call was to a *WithLimit() method.
538: //   The return value from the *WithLimit() method provides a more precise
539: //   disposition.
540: // - The limit is exclusive for forward and inclusive for reverse.
541: //
542: //
543: // Limited iteration mode & range keys
544: //
545: // Limited iteration interacts with range-key iteration. When range key
546: // iteration is enabled, range keys are interleaved at their start boundaries.
547: // Limited iteration must ensure that if a range key exists within the limit,
548: // the iterator visits the range key.
549: //
550: // During forward limited iteration, this is trivial: An overlapping range key
551: // must have a start boundary less than the limit, and the range key's start
552: // boundary will be interleaved and found to be within the limit.
553: //
554: // During reverse limited iteration, the tail of the range key may fall within
555: // the limit. The range key must be surfaced even if the range key's start
556: // boundary is less than the limit, and if there are no point keys between the
557: // current iterator position and the limit. To provide this guarantee, reverse
558: // limited iteration ignores the limit as long as there is a range key
559: // overlapping the iteration position.

586: func (i *Iterator) findNextEntry(limit []byte) {
587: 	i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
588: 	i.pos = iterPosCurForward
589: 	if i.opts.rangeKeys() && i.rangeKey != nil {
590: 		i.rangeKey.rangeKeyOnly = false
591: 	}
592: 
593: 	// Close the closer for the current value if one was open.
594: 	if i.closeValueCloser() != nil {
595: 		return
596: 	}
597: 
598: 	for i.iterKV != nil {
599: 		key := i.iterKV.K
600: 
601: 		// The topLevelIterator.StrictSeekPrefixGE contract requires that in
602: 		// prefix mode [i.hasPrefix=t], every point key returned by the internal
603: 		// iterator must have the current iteration prefix.
604: 		if invariants.Enabled && i.hasPrefix {
605: 			// Range keys are an exception to the contract and may return a different
606: 			// prefix. This case is explicitly handled in the switch statement below.
607: 			if key.Kind() != base.InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet {
608: 				if p := i.comparer.Split.Prefix(key.UserKey); !i.equal(i.prefixOrFullSeekKey, p) {
609: 					i.opts.logger.Fatalf("pebble: prefix violation: key %q does not have prefix %q\n", key.UserKey, i.prefixOrFullSeekKey)
610: 				}
611: 			}
612: 		}
613: 
614: 		// Compare with limit every time we start at a different user key.
615: 		// Note that given the best-effort contract of limit, we could avoid a
616: 		// comparison in the common case by doing this only after
617: 		// i.nextUserKey is called for the deletes below. However that makes
618: 		// the behavior non-deterministic (since the behavior will vary based
619: 		// on what has been compacted), which makes it hard to test with the
620: 		// metamorphic test. So we forego that performance optimization.
621: 		if limit != nil && i.cmp(limit, i.iterKV.K.UserKey) <= 0 {
622: 			i.iterValidityState = IterAtLimit
623: 			i.pos = iterPosCurForwardPaused
624: 			return
625: 		}
626: 
627: 		// If the user has configured a SkipPoint function, invoke it to see
628: 		// whether we should skip over the current user key.
629: 		if i.opts.SkipPoint != nil && key.Kind() != InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet && i.opts.SkipPoint(i.iterKV.K.UserKey) {
630: 			// NB: We could call nextUserKey, but in some cases the SkipPoint
631: 			// predicate function might be cheaper than nextUserKey's key copy
632: 			// and key comparison. This should be the case for MVCC suffix
633: 			// comparisons, for example. In the future, we could expand the
634: 			// SkipPoint interface to give the implementor more control over
635: 			// whether we skip over just the internal key, the user key, or even
636: 			// the key prefix.
637: 			i.stats.ForwardStepCount[InternalIterCall]++
638: 			i.iterKV = i.iter.Next()
639: 			continue
640: 		}
641: 
642: 		switch key.Kind() {
643: 		case InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet:
644: 			if i.hasPrefix {
645: 				if p := i.comparer.Split.Prefix(key.UserKey); !i.equal(i.prefixOrFullSeekKey, p) {
646: 					return
647: 				}
648: 			}
649: 			// Save the current key.
650: 			i.keyBuf = append(i.keyBuf[:0], key.UserKey...)
651: 			i.key = i.keyBuf
652: 			i.value = base.InternalValue{}
653: 			// There may also be a live point key at this userkey that we have
654: 			// not yet read. We need to find the next entry with this user key
655: 			// to find it. Save the range key so we don't lose it when we Next
656: 			// the underlying iterator.
657: 			i.saveRangeKey()
658: 			pointKeyExists := i.nextPointCurrentUserKey()
659: 			if i.err != nil {
660: 				i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
661: 				return
662: 			}
663: 			i.rangeKey.rangeKeyOnly = !pointKeyExists
664: 			i.iterValidityState = IterValid
665: 			return
666: 
667: 		case InternalKeyKindDelete, InternalKeyKindSingleDelete, InternalKeyKindDeleteSized:
668: 			// NB: treating InternalKeyKindSingleDelete as equivalent to DEL is not
669: 			// only simpler, but is also necessary for correctness due to
670: 			// InternalKeyKindSSTableInternalObsoleteBit.
671: 			i.nextUserKey()
672: 			continue
673: 
674: 		case InternalKeyKindSet, InternalKeyKindSetWithDelete:
675: 			i.keyBuf = append(i.keyBuf[:0], key.UserKey...)
676: 			i.key = i.keyBuf
677: 			i.value = i.iterKV.V
678: 			i.iterValidityState = IterValid
679: 			i.saveRangeKey()
680: 			return
681: 
682: 		case InternalKeyKindMerge:
683: 			// Resolving the merge may advance us to the next point key, which
684: 			// may be covered by a different set of range keys. Save the range
685: 			// key state so we don't lose it.
686: 			i.saveRangeKey()
687: 			if i.mergeForward(key) {
688: 				i.iterValidityState = IterValid
689: 				return
690: 			}
691: 
692: 			// The merge didn't yield a valid key, either because the value
693: 			// merger indicated it should be deleted, or because an error was
694: 			// encountered.
695: 			i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
696: 			if i.err != nil {
697: 				return
698: 			}
699: 			if i.pos != iterPosNext {
700: 				i.nextUserKey()
701: 			}
702: 			if i.closeValueCloser() != nil {
703: 				return
704: 			}
705: 			i.pos = iterPosCurForward
706: 
707: 		default:
708: 			i.err = base.CorruptionErrorf("pebble: invalid internal key kind: %d", errors.Safe(key.Kind()))
709: 			i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
710: 			return
711: 		}
712: 	}
713: 
714: 	// Is iterKey nil due to an error?
715: 	if err := i.iter.Error(); err != nil {
716: 		i.err = err
717: 		i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
718: 	}
719: }

721: func (i *Iterator) nextPointCurrentUserKey() bool {
722: 	// If the user has configured a SkipPoint function and the current user key
723: 	// would be skipped by it, there's no need to step forward looking for a
724: 	// point key. If we were to find one, it should be skipped anyways.
725: 	if i.opts.SkipPoint != nil && i.opts.SkipPoint(i.key) {
726: 		return false
727: 	}
728: 
729: 	i.pos = iterPosCurForward
730: 
731: 	i.iterKV = i.iter.Next()
732: 	i.stats.ForwardStepCount[InternalIterCall]++
733: 	if i.iterKV == nil {
734: 		if err := i.iter.Error(); err != nil {
735: 			i.err = err
736: 		} else {
737: 			i.pos = iterPosNext
738: 		}
739: 		return false
740: 	}
741: 	if !i.equal(i.key, i.iterKV.K.UserKey) {
742: 		i.pos = iterPosNext
743: 		return false
744: 	}
745: 
746: 	key := i.iterKV.K
747: 	switch key.Kind() {
748: 	case InternalKeyKindRangeKeySet:
749: 		// RangeKeySets must always be interleaved as the first internal key
750: 		// for a user key.
751: 		i.err = base.CorruptionErrorf("pebble: unexpected range key set mid-user key")
752: 		return false
753: 
754: 	case InternalKeyKindDelete, InternalKeyKindSingleDelete, InternalKeyKindDeleteSized:
755: 		// NB: treating InternalKeyKindSingleDelete as equivalent to DEL is not
756: 		// only simpler, but is also necessary for correctness due to
757: 		// InternalKeyKindSSTableInternalObsoleteBit.
758: 		return false
759: 
760: 	case InternalKeyKindSet, InternalKeyKindSetWithDelete:
761: 		i.value = i.iterKV.V
762: 		return true
763: 
764: 	case InternalKeyKindMerge:
765: 		return i.mergeForward(key)
766: 
767: 	default:
768: 		i.err = base.CorruptionErrorf("pebble: invalid internal key kind: %d", errors.Safe(key.Kind()))
769: 		return false
770: 	}
771: }

773: // mergeForward resolves a MERGE key, advancing the underlying iterator forward
774: // to merge with subsequent keys with the same userkey. mergeForward returns a
775: // boolean indicating whether or not the merge yielded a valid key. A merge may
776: // not yield a valid key if an error occurred, in which case i.err is non-nil,
777: // or the user's value merger specified the key to be deleted.
778: //
779: // mergeForward does not update iterValidityState.
780: func (i *Iterator) mergeForward(key base.InternalKey) (valid bool) {
781: 	var iterValue []byte
782: 	iterValue, _, i.err = i.iterKV.Value(nil)
783: 	if i.err != nil {
784: 		return false
785: 	}
786: 	var valueMerger ValueMerger
787: 	valueMerger, i.err = i.merge(key.UserKey, iterValue)
788: 	if i.err != nil {
789: 		return false
790: 	}
791: 
792: 	i.mergeNext(key, valueMerger)
793: 	if i.err != nil {
794: 		return false
795: 	}
796: 
797: 	var needDelete bool
798: 	var value []byte
799: 	value, needDelete, i.valueCloser, i.err = finishValueMerger(
800: 		valueMerger, true /* includesBase */)
801: 	i.value = base.MakeInPlaceValue(value)
802: 	if i.err != nil {
803: 		return false
804: 	}
805: 	if needDelete {
806: 		_ = i.closeValueCloser()
807: 		return false
808: 	}
809: 	return true
810: }

820: func (i *Iterator) nextUserKey() {
821: 	if i.iterKV == nil {
822: 		return
823: 	}
824: 	trailer := i.iterKV.K.Trailer
825: 	done := i.iterKV.K.Trailer <= base.InternalKeyZeroSeqnumMaxTrailer
826: 	if i.iterValidityState != IterValid {
827: 		i.keyBuf = append(i.keyBuf[:0], i.iterKV.K.UserKey...)
828: 		i.key = i.keyBuf
829: 	}
830: 	for {
831: 		i.stats.ForwardStepCount[InternalIterCall]++
832: 		i.iterKV = i.iter.Next()
833: 		if i.iterKV == nil {
834: 			if err := i.iter.Error(); err != nil {
835: 				i.err = err
836: 				return
837: 			}
838: 		}
839: 		// NB: We're guaranteed to be on the next user key if the previous key
840: 		// had a zero sequence number (`done`), or the new key has a trailer
841: 		// greater or equal to the previous key's trailer. This is true because
842: 		// internal keys with the same user key are sorted by InternalKeyTrailer in
843: 		// strictly monotonically descending order. We expect the trailer
844: 		// optimization to trigger around 50% of the time with randomly
845: 		// distributed writes. We expect it to trigger very frequently when
846: 		// iterating through ingested sstables, which contain keys that all have
847: 		// the same sequence number.
848: 		if done || i.iterKV == nil || i.iterKV.K.Trailer >= trailer {
849: 			break
850: 		}
851: 		if !i.equal(i.key, i.iterKV.K.UserKey) {
852: 			break
853: 		}
854: 		done = i.iterKV.K.Trailer <= base.InternalKeyZeroSeqnumMaxTrailer
855: 		trailer = i.iterKV.K.Trailer
856: 	}
857: }

859: func (i *Iterator) maybeSampleRead() {
860: 	// This method is only called when a public method of Iterator is
861: 	// returning, and below we exclude the case were the iterator is paused at
862: 	// a limit. The effect of these choices is that keys that are deleted, but
863: 	// are encountered during iteration, are not accounted for in the read
864: 	// sampling and will not cause read driven compactions, even though we are
865: 	// incurring cost in iterating over them. And this issue is not limited to
866: 	// Iterator, which does not see the effect of range deletes, which may be
867: 	// causing iteration work in mergingIter. It is not clear at this time
868: 	// whether this is a deficiency worth addressing.
869: 	if i.iterValidityState != IterValid {
870: 		return
871: 	}
872: 	if i.readState == nil {
873: 		return
874: 	}
875: 	if i.readSampling.forceReadSampling {
876: 		i.sampleRead()
877: 		return
878: 	}
879: 	samplingPeriod := int32(int64(readBytesPeriod) * i.readState.db.opts.ReadSamplingMultiplier)
880: 	if samplingPeriod <= 0 {
881: 		return
882: 	}
883: 	bytesRead := uint64(len(i.key) + i.value.Len())
884: 	for i.readSampling.bytesUntilReadSampling < bytesRead {
885: 		i.readSampling.bytesUntilReadSampling += uint64(rand.Uint32N(2 * uint32(samplingPeriod)))
886: 		// The block below tries to adjust for the case where this is the
887: 		// first read in a newly-opened iterator. As bytesUntilReadSampling
888: 		// starts off at zero, we don't want to sample the first read of
889: 		// every newly-opened iterator, but we do want to sample some of them.
890: 		if !i.readSampling.initialSamplePassed {
891: 			i.readSampling.initialSamplePassed = true
892: 			if i.readSampling.bytesUntilReadSampling > bytesRead {
893: 				if rand.Uint64N(i.readSampling.bytesUntilReadSampling) > bytesRead {
894: 					continue
895: 				}
896: 			}
897: 		}
898: 		i.sampleRead()
899: 	}
900: 	i.readSampling.bytesUntilReadSampling -= bytesRead
901: }

903: func (i *Iterator) sampleRead() {
904: 	var topFile *manifest.TableMetadata
905: 	topLevel, numOverlappingLevels := numLevels, 0
906: 	mi := i.merging
907: 	if mi == nil {
908: 		return
909: 	}
910: 	if len(mi.levels) > 1 {
911: 		mi.ForEachLevelIter(func(li *levelIter) (done bool) {
912: 			if li.layer.IsFlushableIngests() {
913: 				return false
914: 			}
915: 			l := li.layer.Level()
916: 			if f := li.iterFile; f != nil {
917: 				var containsKey bool
918: 				if i.pos == iterPosNext || i.pos == iterPosCurForward ||
919: 					i.pos == iterPosCurForwardPaused {
920: 					containsKey = i.cmp(f.PointKeyBounds.SmallestUserKey(), i.key) <= 0
921: 				} else if i.pos == iterPosPrev || i.pos == iterPosCurReverse ||
922: 					i.pos == iterPosCurReversePaused {
923: 					containsKey = i.cmp(f.PointKeyBounds.LargestUserKey(), i.key) >= 0
924: 				}
925: 				// Do nothing if the current key is not contained in f's
926: 				// bounds. We could seek the LevelIterator at this level
927: 				// to find the right file, but the performance impacts of
928: 				// doing that are significant enough to negate the benefits
929: 				// of read sampling in the first place. See the discussion
930: 				// at:
931: 				// https://github.com/cockroachdb/pebble/pull/1041#issuecomment-763226492
932: 				if containsKey {
933: 					numOverlappingLevels++
934: 					if numOverlappingLevels >= 2 {
935: 						// Terminate the loop early if at least 2 overlapping levels are found.
936: 						return true
937: 					}
938: 					topLevel = l
939: 					topFile = f
940: 				}
941: 			}
942: 			return false
943: 		})
944: 	}
945: 	if topFile == nil || topLevel >= numLevels {
946: 		return
947: 	}
948: 	if numOverlappingLevels >= 2 {
949: 		allowedSeeks := topFile.AllowedSeeks.Add(-1)
950: 		if allowedSeeks == 0 {
951: 
952: 			// Since the compaction queue can handle duplicates, we can keep
953: 			// adding to the queue even once allowedSeeks hits 0.
954: 			// In fact, we NEED to keep adding to the queue, because the queue
955: 			// is small and evicts older and possibly useful compactions.
956: 			topFile.AllowedSeeks.Add(topFile.InitAllowedSeeks)
957: 
958: 			read := readCompaction{
959: 				start:    topFile.PointKeyBounds.SmallestUserKey(),
960: 				end:      topFile.PointKeyBounds.LargestUserKey(),
961: 				level:    topLevel,
962: 				tableNum: topFile.TableNum,
963: 			}
964: 			i.readSampling.pendingCompactions.add(&read, i.cmp)
965: 		}
966: 	}
967: }

969: func (i *Iterator) findPrevEntry(limit []byte) {
970: 	i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
971: 	i.pos = iterPosCurReverse
972: 	if i.opts.rangeKeys() && i.rangeKey != nil {
973: 		i.rangeKey.rangeKeyOnly = false
974: 	}
975: 
976: 	// Close the closer for the current value if one was open.
977: 	if i.valueCloser != nil {
978: 		i.err = i.valueCloser.Close()
979: 		i.valueCloser = nil
980: 		if i.err != nil {
981: 			i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
982: 			return
983: 		}
984: 	}
985: 
986: 	var valueMerger ValueMerger
987: 	firstLoopIter := true
988: 	rangeKeyBoundary := false
989: 	// The code below compares with limit in multiple places. As documented in
990: 	// findNextEntry, this is being done to make the behavior of limit
991: 	// deterministic to allow for metamorphic testing. It is not required by
992: 	// the best-effort contract of limit.
993: 	for i.iterKV != nil {
994: 		key := i.iterKV.K
995: 
996: 		// NB: We cannot pause if the current key is covered by a range key.
997: 		// Otherwise, the user might not ever learn of a range key that covers
998: 		// the key space being iterated over in which there are no point keys.
999: 		// Since limits are best effort, ignoring the limit in this case is
1000: 		// allowed by the contract of limit.
1001: 		if firstLoopIter && limit != nil && i.cmp(limit, i.iterKV.K.UserKey) > 0 && !i.rangeKeyWithinLimit(limit) {
1002: 			i.iterValidityState = IterAtLimit
1003: 			i.pos = iterPosCurReversePaused
1004: 			return
1005: 		}
1006: 		firstLoopIter = false
1007: 
1008: 		if i.iterValidityState == IterValid {
1009: 			if !i.equal(key.UserKey, i.key) {
1010: 				// We've iterated to the previous user key.
1011: 				i.pos = iterPosPrev
1012: 				if valueMerger != nil {
1013: 					var needDelete bool
1014: 					var value []byte
1015: 					value, needDelete, i.valueCloser, i.err = finishValueMerger(valueMerger, true /* includesBase */)
1016: 					i.value = base.MakeInPlaceValue(value)
1017: 					if i.err == nil && needDelete {
1018: 						// The point key at this key is deleted. If we also have
1019: 						// a range key boundary at this key, we still want to
1020: 						// return. Otherwise, we need to continue looking for
1021: 						// a live key.
1022: 						i.value = base.InternalValue{}
1023: 						if rangeKeyBoundary {
1024: 							i.rangeKey.rangeKeyOnly = true
1025: 						} else {
1026: 							i.iterValidityState = IterExhausted
1027: 							if i.closeValueCloser() == nil {
1028: 								continue
1029: 							}
1030: 						}
1031: 					}
1032: 				}

14: // FragmentIterator defines an iterator interface over spans. The spans
15: // surfaced by a FragmentIterator must be non-overlapping. This is achieved by
16: // fragmenting spans at overlap points (see Fragmenter).
17: //
18: // A Span returned by a FragmentIterator is only valid until the next
19: // positioning method. Some implementations (eg, keyspan.Iter) may provide
20: // longer lifetimes but implementations need only guarantee stability until the
21: // next positioning method.
22: //
23: // If any positioning method fails to find a span, the iterator is left
24: // positioned at an exhausted position in the direction of iteration. For
25: // example, a caller than finds SeekGE(k)=nil may call Prev to move the iterator
26: // to the last span.
27: //
28: // If an error occurs during any positioning method, the method returns a nil
29: // span and a non-nil error.
30: type FragmentIterator interface {
31: 	// SeekGE moves the iterator to the first span covering a key greater than
32: 	// or equal to the given key. This is equivalent to seeking to the first
33: 	// span with an end key greater than the given key.
34: 	SeekGE(key []byte) (*Span, error)
35: 
36: 	// SeekLT moves the iterator to the last span covering a key less than the
37: 	// given key. This is equivalent to seeking to the last span with a start
38: 	// key less than the given key.
39: 	SeekLT(key []byte) (*Span, error)
40: 
41: 	// First moves the iterator to the first span.
42: 	First() (*Span, error)
43: 
44: 	// Last moves the iterator to the last span.
45: 	Last() (*Span, error)
46: 
47: 	// Next moves the iterator to the next span.
48: 	//
49: 	// It is valid to call Next when the iterator is positioned before the first
50: 	// key/value pair due to either a prior call to SeekLT or Prev which
51: 	// returned an invalid span. It is not allowed to call Next when the
52: 	// previous call to SeekGE or Next returned an invalid span.
53: 	Next() (*Span, error)
54: 
55: 	// Prev moves the iterator to the previous span.
56: 	//
57: 	// It is valid to call Prev when the iterator is positioned after the last
58: 	// key/value pair due to either a prior call to SeekGE or Next which
59: 	// returned an invalid span. It is not allowed to call Prev when the
60: 	// previous call to SeekLT or Prev returned an invalid span.
61: 	Prev() (*Span, error)
62: 
63: 	// Close closes the iterator. It is not in general valid to call Close
64: 	// multiple times. Other methods should not be called after the iterator has
65: 	// been closed. Spans returned by a previous method should also not be used
66: 	// after the iterator has been closed.
67: 	Close()
68: 
69: 	// WrapChildren wraps any child iterators using the given function. The
70: 	// function can call WrapChildren to recursively wrap an entire iterator
71: 	// stack. Used only for debug logging.
72: 	WrapChildren(wrap WrapFn)
73: 
74: 	// SetContext replaces the context provided at iterator creation, or the last
75: 	// one provided by SetContext.
76: 	SetContext(ctx context.Context)

120: // SeekGE implements FragmentIterator.SeekGE.
121: func (i *Iter) SeekGE(key []byte) (*Span, error) {
122: 	// NB: manually inlined sort.Search is ~5% faster.
123: 	//
124: 	// Define f(j) = false iff the span i.spans[j] is strictly before `key`
125: 	// (equivalently, i.spans[j].End ≤ key.)
126: 	//
127: 	// Define f(-1) == false and f(n) == true.
128: 	// Invariant: f(index-1) == false, f(upper) == true.
129: 	i.index = 0
130: 	upper := len(i.spans)
131: 	for i.index < upper {
132: 		h := int(uint(i.index+upper) >> 1) // avoid overflow when computing h
133: 		// i.index ≤ h < upper
134: 		if i.cmp(key, i.spans[h].End) >= 0 {
135: 			i.index = h + 1 // preserves f(i-1) == false
136: 		} else {
137: 			upper = h // preserves f(j) == true
138: 		}
139: 	}
140: 
141: 	// i.index == upper, f(i.index-1) == false, and f(upper) (= f(i.index)) ==
142: 	// true => answer is i.index.
143: 	if i.index >= len(i.spans) {
144: 		return nil, nil
145: 	}
146: 	return &i.spans[i.index], nil
147: }
148: 
149: // SeekLT implements FragmentIterator.SeekLT.
150: func (i *Iter) SeekLT(key []byte) (*Span, error) {
151: 	// NB: manually inlined sort.Search is ~5% faster.
152: 	//
153: 	// Define f(-1) == false and f(n) == true.
154: 	// Invariant: f(index-1) == false, f(upper) == true.
155: 	i.index = 0
156: 	upper := len(i.spans)
157: 	for i.index < upper {
158: 		h := int(uint(i.index+upper) >> 1) // avoid overflow when computing h
159: 		// i.index ≤ h < upper
160: 		if i.cmp(key, i.spans[h].Start) > 0 {
161: 			i.index = h + 1 // preserves f(i-1) == false
162: 		} else {
163: 			upper = h // preserves f(j) == true
164: 		}
165: 	}
166: 	// i.index == upper, f(i.index-1) == false, and f(upper) (= f(i.index)) ==
167: 	// true => answer is i.index.
168: 
169: 	// Since keys are strictly increasing, if i.index > 0 then i.index-1 will be
170: 	// the largest whose key is < the key sought.
171: 	i.index--
172: 	if i.index < 0 {
173: 		return nil, nil
174: 	}
175: 	return &i.spans[i.index], nil
176: }

178: // First implements FragmentIterator.First.
179: func (i *Iter) First() (*Span, error) {
180: 	if len(i.spans) == 0 {
181: 		return nil, nil
182: 	}
183: 	i.index = 0
184: 	return &i.spans[i.index], nil

189: 	if len(i.spans) == 0 {

192: 	i.index = len(i.spans) - 1

198: 	if i.index >= len(i.spans) {
199: 		return nil, nil
200: 	}
201: 	i.index++
202: 	if i.index >= len(i.spans) {
203: 		return nil, nil
204: 	}
205: 	return &i.spans[i.index], nil
206: }

68: // flushableEntry wraps a flushable and adds additional metadata and

70: type flushableEntry struct {
71: 	flushable
72: 	// Channel which is closed when the flushable has been flushed.
73: 	flushed chan struct{}
74: 	// flushForced indicates whether a flush was forced on this memtable (either
75: 	// manual, or due to ingestion). Protected by DB.mu.
76: 	flushForced bool
77: 	// delayedFlushForcedAt indicates whether a timer has been set to force a
78: 	// flush on this memtable at some point in the future. Protected by DB.mu.
79: 	// Holds the timestamp of when the flush will be issued.
80: 	delayedFlushForcedAt time.Time
81: 	// logNum corresponds to the WAL that contains the records present in the
82: 	// receiver. It is possible for multiple flushable entries to have the same
83: 	// logNum:
84: 	// 1. When a large batch is committed, it is not appended to the WAL.
85: 	// Instead, the memtable is rotated, and the large batch is appended to the
86: 	// flushable queue with a logNum that matches the newly immutable memtable.
87: 	// Care is taken in DB.flush1 to ensure that the large batch is always
88: 	// flushed alongside the memtable with the same logNum.
89: 	// 2. During recovery, we replay WAL entries into the mutable memtable. The
90: 	// memtable we allocate during recovery may be smaller than the memtable
91: 	// that corresponded to the original WAL at the time it was written. This
92: 	// means we may fill the memtable before finishing replaying the WAL,
93: 	// resulting in multiple consecutive flushable entries all with the same
94: 	// logNum. This is okay because we take care to flush all the flushables
95: 	// during Open.
96: 	logNum base.DiskFileNum
97: 	// logSize is the size in bytes of the associated WAL. Protected by DB.mu.
98: 	logSize uint64
99: 	// The current logSeqNum at the time the memtable was created. This is
100: 	// guaranteed to be less than or equal to any seqnum stored in the memtable.
101: 	logSeqNum base.SeqNum
102: 	// readerRefs tracks the read references on the flushable. The two sources of
103: 	// reader references are DB.mu.mem.queue and readState.memtables. The memory
104: 	// reserved by the flushable in the cache is released when the reader refs
105: 	// drop to zero. If the flushable is referencing sstables, then the file
106: 	// refcount is also decreased once the reader refs drops to 0. If the
107: 	// flushable is a memTable, when the reader refs drops to zero, the writer
108: 	// refs will already be zero because the memtable will have been flushed and
109: 	// that only occurs once the writer refs drops to zero.
110: 	readerRefs atomic.Int32
111: 	// Closure to invoke to release memory accounting.
112: 	releaseMemAccounting func()
113: 	// unrefFiles, if not nil, should be invoked to decrease the ref count of
114: 	// files which are backing the flushable.
115: 	unrefFiles func(*manifest.ObsoleteFiles)
116: 	// deleteFnLocked should be called if the caller is holding DB.mu.
117: 	deleteFnLocked func(manifest.ObsoleteFiles)
118: 	// deleteFn should be called if the caller is not holding DB.mu.
119: 	deleteFn func(manifest.ObsoleteFiles)
120: }
